steps.title: 쉬는 날 뭐 해요?
steps.title_en: What do you do in your free time?
steps.goal: 취미를 깊이 묻고 얼마나 자주 하는지 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 월요일 점심, 회사 탕비실. 작은 테이블에서 도시락을 먹는 지우에게 클로이가 휴대폰 속 실내 암벽장 사진을 신나게 보여 줌
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What do you do in your free time?" (쉬는 날 뭐 해요?). Goal: 취미를 깊이 묻고 얼마나 자주 하는지 말하기. Today's scene: 12월 월요일 점심, 회사 탕비실. 작은 테이블에서 도시락을 먹는 지우에게 클로이가 휴대폰 속 실내 암벽장 사진을 신나게 보여 줌. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What do you do in your free time?".

steps.en: What do you do in your free time?
steps.when: 상대의 취미를 물을 때 써요. free time은 일이나 공부가 없는 시간이에요.
steps.extra: 대답: I do yoga. · I go hiking.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What do you do in your free time?" (시간 날 때 뭐 해요?). When to use it: 상대의 취미를 물을 때 써요. free time은 일이나 공부가 없는 시간이에요. Note: 대답: I do yoga. · I go hiking.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’m really into ___.".

steps.when: 요즘 아주 좋아하는 것을 말해요. into 뒤에는 명사나 *-ing*.
steps.extra: I’m really into drawing. · I’m into yoga.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’m really into ___." (~에 푹 빠졌어요.). When to use it: 요즘 아주 좋아하는 것을 말해요. into 뒤에는 명사나 -ing. Note: I’m really into drawing. · I’m into yoga.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "How often do you ___?".

steps.when: 몇 번 하는지 물어요.
steps.extra: 대답: Once a week. · Almost every day.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "How often do you ___?" (얼마나 자주 ~해요?). When to use it: 몇 번 하는지 물어요. Note: 대답: Once a week. · Almost every day.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Lunch Break Talk · 월요일 점심, 회사 탕비실에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Lunch Break Talk · 월요일 점심, 회사 탕비실에서

lines.en: Ooh, that looks good! Hey, Jiwoo. {{What do you do in your free time}}?
lines.ko: 오, 맛있겠다! 참, 지우 씨. 시간 날 때 뭐 해요?

lines.en: I do yoga. {{I’m really into}} it these days.
lines.ko: 요가 해요. 요즘 요가에 푹 빠졌어요.

lines.en: “I’m really into it.” That sounded so natural! {{How often do you}} go?
lines.ko: “I’m really into it.” 정말 자연스러웠어요! 얼마나 자주 가요?

lines.en: Once a week. It helps me relax. What about you?
lines.ko: 일주일에 한 번요. 마음이 편해져요. 클로이는요?

lines.en: I love drawing. I draw almost every day. And I’ve just started climbing!
lines.ko: 저는 그림 그리기를 좋아해요. 거의 매일 그려요. 그리고 얼마 전에 암벽 등반을 시작했어요!

lines.en: Climbing? Wow! How did you get into it?
lines.ko: 등반이요? 와! 어떻게 시작하게 됐어요?

lines.en: A friend got me into it. Now I’m a member of an indoor climbing club.
lines.ko: 친구 덕분에 빠졌어요. 이제 실내 암벽 등반 동호회 회원이에요.

lines.en: Is it hard?
lines.ko: 어려워요?

lines.en: Yes! I’m not very good at it. I usually come down after a few meters.
lines.ko: 네! 아직 잘 못해요. 보통 몇 미터 올라가다 내려와요.

lines.en: Ha! {{How often do you}} go?
lines.ko: 하하! 얼마나 자주 가요?

lines.en: Not very often. Just on Thursdays. You should come with me sometime. Come on!
lines.ko: 자주는 아니에요. 목요일에만요. 언제 저랑 같이 가요. 자, 어서요!

lines.en: Hmm… okay! I’ll come to the club this Thursday.
lines.ko: 음… 좋아요! 이번 목요일에 동호회에 가 볼게요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Lunch Break Talk · 월요일 점심, 회사 탕비실에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Chloe: "Ooh, that looks good! Hey, Jiwoo. What do you do in your free time?" (오, 맛있겠다! 참, 지우 씨. 시간 날 때 뭐 해요?)
2. Jiwoo: "I do yoga. I’m really into it these days." (요가 해요. 요즘 요가에 푹 빠졌어요.)
3. Chloe: "“I’m really into it.” That sounded so natural! How often do you go?" (“I’m really into it.” 정말 자연스러웠어요! 얼마나 자주 가요?)
4. Jiwoo: "Once a week. It helps me relax. What about you?" (일주일에 한 번요. 마음이 편해져요. 클로이는요?)
5. Chloe: "I love drawing. I draw almost every day. And I’ve just started climbing!" (저는 그림 그리기를 좋아해요. 거의 매일 그려요. 그리고 얼마 전에 암벽 등반을 시작했어요!)
6. Jiwoo: "Climbing? Wow! How did you get into it?" (등반이요? 와! 어떻게 시작하게 됐어요?)
7. Chloe: "A friend got me into it. Now I’m a member of an indoor climbing club." (친구 덕분에 빠졌어요. 이제 실내 암벽 등반 동호회 회원이에요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Is it hard?" (어려워요?)
9. Chloe: "Yes! I’m not very good at it. I usually come down after a few meters." (네! 아직 잘 못해요. 보통 몇 미터 올라가다 내려와요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Ha! How often do you go?" (하하! 얼마나 자주 가요?)
11. Chloe: "Not very often. Just on Thursdays. You should come with me sometime. Come on!" (자주는 아니에요. 목요일에만요. 언제 저랑 같이 가요. 자, 어서요!)
12. Jiwoo: "Hmm… okay! I’ll come to the club this Thursday." (음… 좋아요! 이번 목요일에 동호회에 가 볼게요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.

frame: What do you do in your free time? / How often do you ___?
I’m really into ___. / Once a week.
head: 취미 (I’m into …)
얼마나 자주
이렇게 말해요
rows: once a week 일주일에 한 번
I’m into yoga. I go once a week.
I’m really into drawing. I draw almost every day.
twice a month 한 달에 두 번
I’m into hiking. I go twice a month.
I like fishing, but I don’t go very often.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What do you do in your free time? / How often do you ___? / I’m really into ___. / Once a week. Table (취미 (I’m into …) → 얼마나 자주):
- yoga 요가 → once a week 일주일에 한 번
- drawing 그림 그리기 → almost every day 거의 매일
- hiking 등산 → twice a month 한 달에 두 번
- fishing 낚시 → not very often 자주는 아님
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
*How often* do you go? 얼마나 자주 가요?
*once* a week 일주일에 한 번 · *twice* a week 두 번
*three times* a week 세 번
한 번·두 번만 once·twice, 셋부터는 ___ times.

I’m *into* yoga. 요가에 빠져 있어요.
into 뒤에는 명사나 -ing: She’s *into* drawing.
더 강하게: I’m *really* into it.
빠지게 된 계기는 get into: How did you get into it?
errors: I go to yoga once week.
I go to yoga once a week.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- How often ~? 얼마나 자주: How often do you go? 얼마나 자주 가요? / once a week 일주일에 한 번 · twice a week 두 번 / three times a week 세 번 / 한 번·두 번만 once·twice, 셋부터는 ___ times.
- be into ~ 푹 빠져 있다: I’m into yoga. 요가에 빠져 있어요. / into 뒤에는 명사나 -ing: She’s into drawing. / 더 강하게: I’m really into it. / 빠지게 된 계기는 get into: How did you get into it?
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’m really into draw. → I’m really into drawing. (into 뒤에는 명사나 -ing를 써요.)
- I really into yoga. → I’m really into yoga. (be동사(’m)를 빼지 않아요.)
- How often you go? → How often do you go? (물을 때는 do를 넣어요.)
- I go to yoga once week. → I go to yoga once a week. (week 앞에 a를 넣어요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) yoga / once a week → I’m really into yoga. I go once a week. · 선생님이 How often do you ___? 하고 물으면 바로 대답해요.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) yoga / once a week → I’m really into yoga. I go once a week. · 선생님이 How often do you ___? 하고 물으면 바로 대답해요. Items (situation → model answer): yoga → once a week | drawing → almost every day | cooking → three times a week | gardening → twice a month.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: What do you do in your free time?
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "What do you do in your free time?" (쉬는 날 뭐 해요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What do you do in your free time?" / "I’m really into ___." / "How often do you ___?". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: How did you get into it?

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 얼마나 자주: "Once a week." (일주일에 한 번요., 보통); "Almost every day." (거의 매일요., 보통); "Not very often." (자주는 아니에요., 보통)
- 계기 묻고 답하기: "How did you get into it?" (어떻게 시작하게 됐어요?, 친근); "A friend got me into it." (친구 덕분에 빠졌어요., 친근); "I’ve just started ___." (얼마 전에 ~를 시작했어요., 보통)

Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What do you do in your free time?" (hint on screen: I’m really into ___. / I like ___.)
- "How often do you do it?" (hint on screen: Once a week. / Almost every day. / Not very often.)
- "How did you get into it?" (hint on screen: A friend got me into it. / I’ve just started it.)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. steps.title: Chloe’s Climbing Club
steps.text: Chloe joined an indoor climbing club last month. The membership is fairly cheap, and the club has many activities, like a craft night. Climbing fascinates her. She generally goes on Thursdays, *as soon as* she finishes work. The members are interesting. One is a musician and plays three instruments. Another is a singer. One member even has a collection of poems about climbing! For Chloe, every climb is a small victory. On weekends, some members go hiking on mountain trails. Jiwoo is curious now. She wants to *come to* the club this Thursday.

What does Jiwoo want to do?

steps.title: 어떻게 생각해요?
steps.title_en: What do you think about it?
steps.goal: 생각을 묻고, 말하고, 동의하거나 반대하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 평일 점심, 회사 근처 작은 식당 창가 자리. 국숫그릇을 앞에 둔 마야가 손짓하며 말하고, 지우가 고개를 갸웃하며 듣고 있음
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What do you think about it?" (어떻게 생각해요?). Goal: 생각을 묻고, 말하고, 동의하거나 반대하기. Today's scene: 12월 평일 점심, 회사 근처 작은 식당 창가 자리. 국숫그릇을 앞에 둔 마야가 손짓하며 말하고, 지우가 고개를 갸웃하며 듣고 있음. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What do you think about ___?".

steps.when: 상대의 생각(의견)을 물을 때 써요.
steps.extra: What do you think about working from home?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What do you think about ___?" (~에 대해 어떻게 생각해요?). When to use it: 상대의 생각(의견)을 물을 때 써요. Note: What do you think about working from home?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I think ___.".

steps.when: 내 생각을 부드럽게 말해요. think 뒤에 *문장*을 그대로 붙여요.
steps.extra: I think it’s a great idea.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I think ___." (~인 것 같아요.). When to use it: 내 생각을 부드럽게 말해요. think 뒤에 문장을 그대로 붙여요. Note: I think it’s a great idea.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I think so, too. / I don’t think so.".

steps.en: I think so, too. / I don’t think so.
steps.ko: 저도 그렇게 생각해요. / 아닌 것 같아요.
steps.when: 상대 말에 동의하거나 반대할 때 써요.
steps.extra: A: It’s a great idea. B: I think so, too.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I think so, too. / I don’t think so." (저도 그렇게 생각해요. / 아닌 것 같아요.). When to use it: 상대 말에 동의하거나 반대할 때 써요. Note: A: It’s a great idea. B: I think so, too.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Home or Office? · 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Home or Office? · 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, my company is trying something new. We can work from home two days a week.
lines.ko: 지우, 우리 회사가 새로운 걸 시험해 보고 있어요. 일주일에 이틀은 집에서 일할 수 있어요.

lines.en: Oh, really? {{What do you think about}} it?
lines.ko: 오, 정말요? 마야는 그거 어떻게 생각해요?

lines.en: {{I think}} it’s a great idea. No crowded subway in the morning!
lines.ko: 좋은 생각 같아요. 아침에 붐비는 지하철을 안 타도 돼요!

lines.en: {{I think so, too}}. But is it good for the team? Hmm…
lines.ko: 저도 그렇게 생각해요. 그런데 팀한테도 좋을까요? 음…

lines.en: You’ve got this! Tell me your opinion.
lines.ko: 할 수 있어요! 지우 의견을 말해 봐요.

lines.en: Well, I think a team needs time together.
lines.ko: 음, 팀은 같이 있는 시간이 필요한 것 같아요.

lines.en: Why do you think so?
lines.ko: 왜 그렇게 생각해요?

lines.en: Good ideas often come at lunch or by the coffee machine.
lines.ko: 좋은 아이디어는 점심 때나 커피 머신 옆에서 자주 나오잖아요.

lines.en: Good point. But my boss is worried. He thinks people just relax at home.
lines.ko: 좋은 지적이에요. 그런데 우리 상사는 걱정해요. 사람들이 집에서 그냥 쉰다고 생각해요.

lines.en: {{I don’t think so}}. Many people work hard at home.
lines.ko: 저는 그렇게 생각 안 해요. 많은 사람이 집에서도 열심히 일해요.

lines.en: You’re right. Oh, and my heating bill may well go up this winter!
lines.ko: 맞아요. 아, 그리고 이번 겨울엔 난방비가 오를 것 같아요!

lines.en: That’s true! Make sure you wear a warm sweater.
lines.ko: 그렇겠네요! 따뜻한 스웨터 꼭 입어요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Home or Office? · 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Maya: "Jiwoo, my company is trying something new. We can work from home two days a week." (지우, 우리 회사가 새로운 걸 시험해 보고 있어요. 일주일에 이틀은 집에서 일할 수 있어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Oh, really? What do you think about it?" (오, 정말요? 마야는 그거 어떻게 생각해요?)
3. Maya: "I think it’s a great idea. No crowded subway in the morning!" (좋은 생각 같아요. 아침에 붐비는 지하철을 안 타도 돼요!)
4. Jiwoo: "I think so, too. But is it good for the team? Hmm…" (저도 그렇게 생각해요. 그런데 팀한테도 좋을까요? 음…)
5. Maya: "You’ve got this! Tell me your opinion." (할 수 있어요! 지우 의견을 말해 봐요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Well, I think a team needs time together." (음, 팀은 같이 있는 시간이 필요한 것 같아요.)
7. Maya: "Why do you think so?" (왜 그렇게 생각해요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Good ideas often come at lunch or by the coffee machine." (좋은 아이디어는 점심 때나 커피 머신 옆에서 자주 나오잖아요.)
9. Maya: "Good point. But my boss is worried. He thinks people just relax at home." (좋은 지적이에요. 그런데 우리 상사는 걱정해요. 사람들이 집에서 그냥 쉰다고 생각해요.)
10. Jiwoo: "I don’t think so. Many people work hard at home." (저는 그렇게 생각 안 해요. 많은 사람이 집에서도 열심히 일해요.)
11. Maya: "You’re right. Oh, and my heating bill may well go up this winter!" (맞아요. 아, 그리고 이번 겨울엔 난방비가 오를 것 같아요!)
12. Jiwoo: "That’s true! Make sure you wear a warm sweater." (그렇겠네요! 따뜻한 스웨터 꼭 입어요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

10. Jiwoo (learner): "I don’t think so. Many people work hard at home." (저는 그렇게 생각 안 해요. 많은 사람이 집에서도 열심히 일해요.)
11. Maya (you): "You’re right. Oh, and my heating bill may well go up this winter!" (맞아요. 아, 그리고 이번 겨울엔 난방비가 오를 것 같아요!)
12. Jiwoo (learner): "That’s true! Make sure you wear a warm sweater." (그렇겠네요! 따뜻한 스웨터 꼭 입어요.)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Maya. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Maya can work from home two days a week.
Maya thinks it’s a bad idea.
Jiwoo thinks a team needs time together.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. Maya can work from home two days a week.
2. Maya thinks it’s a bad idea.
3. Jiwoo thinks a team needs time together.
The scene they are about:
1. Maya: "Jiwoo, my company is trying something new. We can work from home two days a week." (지우, 우리 회사가 새로운 걸 시험해 보고 있어요. 일주일에 이틀은 집에서 일할 수 있어요.)
2. Jiwoo: "Oh, really? What do you think about it?" (오, 정말요? 마야는 그거 어떻게 생각해요?)
3. Maya: "I think it’s a great idea. No crowded subway in the morning!" (좋은 생각 같아요. 아침에 붐비는 지하철을 안 타도 돼요!)
4. Jiwoo: "I think so, too. But is it good for the team? Hmm…" (저도 그렇게 생각해요. 그런데 팀한테도 좋을까요? 음…)
5. Maya: "You’ve got this! Tell me your opinion." (할 수 있어요! 지우 의견을 말해 봐요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Well, I think a team needs time together." (음, 팀은 같이 있는 시간이 필요한 것 같아요.)
7. Maya: "Why do you think so?" (왜 그렇게 생각해요?)
8. Jiwoo: "Good ideas often come at lunch or by the coffee machine." (좋은 아이디어는 점심 때나 커피 머신 옆에서 자주 나오잖아요.)
9. Maya: "Good point. But my boss is worried. He thinks people just relax at home." (좋은 지적이에요. 그런데 우리 상사는 걱정해요. 사람들이 집에서 그냥 쉰다고 생각해요.)
10. Jiwoo: "I don’t think so. Many people work hard at home." (저는 그렇게 생각 안 해요. 많은 사람이 집에서도 열심히 일해요.)
11. Maya: "You’re right. Oh, and my heating bill may well go up this winter!" (맞아요. 아, 그리고 이번 겨울엔 난방비가 오를 것 같아요!)
12. Jiwoo: "That’s true! Make sure you wear a warm sweater." (그렇겠네요! 따뜻한 스웨터 꼭 입어요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: I think ___. / I think so, too. / I don’t think so.
head: 주제 (What do you think about …?)
내 생각 (I think …)
맞장구·반대
rows: I think it’s a great idea.
I think they’re a good idea.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What do you think about ___? / I think ___. / I think so, too. / I don’t think so. Table (주제 (What do you think about …?) → 내 생각 (I think …)):
- working from home 재택근무 → I think it’s a great idea.
- online classes 온라인 수업 → I think they’re fun.
- early meetings 이른 회의 → I think they’re too early.
- lunch meetings 점심 회의 → I think they’re a good idea.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
think 뒤에 *주어+동사* 문장을 그대로 붙여요.
I think *it’s* a great idea.
I think *a team needs* time together.
반대: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

동의: I think so, too. · I agree.
반대: I don’t think so. · I don’t agree.
부드럽게: Maybe you’re right. · Well, it depends.
errors: What do you think about it?
I think it’s a good idea.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- I think + 문장: think 뒤에 주어+동사 문장을 그대로 붙여요. / I think it’s a great idea. / I think a team needs time together. / 반대: I don’t think it’s a good idea.
- 짧게 동의·반대하기: 동의: I think so, too. · I agree. / 반대: I don’t think so. · I don’t agree. / 부드럽게: Maybe you’re right. · Well, it depends.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I am agree. → I agree. (agree는 동사라서 am을 붙이지 않아요.)
- What do you think it? → What do you think about it? (주제 앞에 about을 넣어요.)
- I think it’s good idea. → I think it’s a good idea. (idea 앞에 a를 넣어요.)
- Why you think so? → Why do you think so? (물을 때는 do를 넣어요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: I think + 문장: think 뒤에 주어+동사 문장을 그대로 붙여요.I think it’s a great idea.I think a team needs time together.반대: I don’t think it’s a good idea.

mistakes: I am agree. → I agree.
What do you think it? → What do you think about it?
I think it’s good idea. → I think it’s a good idea.
Why you think so? → Why do you think so?

steps.note: 예) working from home / a great idea → What do you think about working from home? — I think it’s a great idea.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) working from home / a great idea → What do you think about working from home? — I think it’s a great idea. Items (situation → model answer): working from home → a great idea | online classes → fun | early meetings → too early | winter → a nice season.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: I think so, too. / I don’t think so.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "What do you think about it?" (어떻게 생각해요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What do you think about ___?" / "I think ___." / "I think so, too. / I don’t think so.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 동의하기: "I agree." (동의해요., 보통); "You’re right." (맞아요., 보통); "That’s true." (그건 그래요., 보통); "Good point." (좋은 지적이에요., 친근)
- 반대하거나 망설이기: "I don’t agree." (동의하지 않아요., 보통); "Maybe you’re right." (그럴 수도 있겠네요., 정중); "I’m not sure." (잘 모르겠어요., 보통); "Well, it depends." (글쎄요, 경우에 따라 달라요., 보통)
- 이유 묻기: "Why do you think so?" (왜 그렇게 생각해요?, 보통); "What’s your opinion?" (의견이 어때요?, 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 생각을 말할 때 앞에 붙이는 말

*Actually*, … 사실은(뜻밖의 말을 할 때)
*Honestly*, … 솔직히 말하면
*Clearly*, … 분명히 · It’s *unclear*. 아직 확실하지 않아요.
fact 와 opinion

It’s Monday. 사실(*fact*) — 맞다·틀리다가 있어요.
I think Mondays are hard. 의견(*opinion*) — 사람마다 달라요.
*express* an opinion 의견을 말하다 · a *discussion* 의논
steps.blank:
A: What do you ___ about working from home?   B: I ___ it’s a great idea.
A: I think so, ___.   B: Really? Why do you think ___?
낱말 상자: think · think · too · so
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 생각을 말할 때 앞에 붙이는 말: Actually, … 사실은(뜻밖의 말을 할 때) / Honestly, … 솔직히 말하면 / Clearly, … 분명히 · It’s unclear. 아직 확실하지 않아요.
- fact 와 opinion: It’s Monday. 사실(fact) — 맞다·틀리다가 있어요. / I think Mondays are hard. 의견(opinion) — 사람마다 달라요. / express an opinion 의견을 말하다 · a discussion 의논
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What do you ___ about working from home? B: I ___ it’s a great idea. / A: I think so, ___. B: Really? Why do you think ___? / 낱말 상자: think · think · too · so
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: agree (동의하다), disagree (동의하지 않다), opinion (의견), discussion (의논, 토론), express ((생각을) 말하다, 나타내다), point ((말의) 요점), reason (이유), important (중요한), fact (사실), true (사실인, 맞는), mind (마음, 생각), idea (생각, 아이디어).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: It is indeed a big change.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: think (생각하다) — "I think so, too."; right (맞는, 옳은) — "You’re right."; sure (확실한) — "I’m not sure."; well (글쎄, 음) — "Well, it depends."; maybe (아마, 어쩌면) — "Maybe you’re right."; actually (사실은) — "Actually, my home isn’t quiet."; honestly (솔직히) — "Honestly, I miss the office."; clearly (분명히) — "Clearly, people like it."; unclear (확실하지 않은) — "The answer is unclear."; indeed (정말로, 참으로) — "It is indeed a big change.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What do you think about working from home?
I think winter is a great season. Do you agree?
I think so, too. / I don’t think so. / I’m not sure.
What do you think about online English classes?
Ask me my opinion about something.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What do you think about working from home?" (hint on screen: I think ___. / Well, it depends.)
- "I think winter is a great season. Do you agree?" (hint on screen: I think so, too. / I don’t think so. / I’m not sure.)
- "Why do you think so?" (hint on screen: I think ___ because ___.)
- "What do you think about online English classes?" (hint on screen: I think they’re ___.)
- "Ask me my opinion about something." (hint on screen: What do you think about ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: What do you think about working from home?
I think winter is a great season. Do you agree?

steps.title: Maya’s Team Discussion
steps.text: Every Friday, Maya’s team has a short discussion. This week, the topic is working from home. Maya asks everybody to express an opinion. One member agrees with the plan. Another member disagrees. His reason is simple. “It’s important to see faces.” Maya writes down every point. Clearly, people have different opinions about the plan. But some facts are still unclear. For example, heating bills *may well go up*. Maya says, “Let’s try it for a month and *make sure* it works.” It is indeed a big change. Maybe somebody will change their mind!
steps.gloss: discussion 의논 · express an opinion 의견을 말하다 · reason 이유 · clearly 분명히 · unclear 확실하지 않은 · may well 아마 ~할 것이다 · go up 오르다 · make sure 꼭 ~하게 하다 · indeed 정말로 · change one’s mind 생각을 바꾸다
questions: What is the topic of the discussion?
Why does one member disagree?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Maya’s Team Discussion". Text: "Every Friday, Maya’s team has a short discussion. This week, the topic is working from home. Maya asks everybody to express an opinion. One member agrees with the plan. Another member disagrees. His reason is simple. “It’s important to see faces.” Maya writes down every point. Clearly, people have different opinions about the plan. But some facts are still unclear. For example, heating bills may well go up. Maya says, “Let’s try it for a month and make sure it works.” It is indeed a big change. Maybe somebody will change their mind!" Words: discussion 의논 · express an opinion 의견을 말하다 · reason 이유 · clearly 분명히 · unclear 확실하지 않은 · may well 아마 ~할 것이다 · go up 오르다 · make sure 꼭 ~하게 하다 · indeed 정말로 · change one’s mind 생각을 바꾸다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What is the topic of the discussion?" / "Why does one member disagree?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What do you think about ___?’로 상대의 생각을 물을 수 있어요.
‘I think ___.’로 내 생각을 말할 수 있어요.
‘I think so, too. / I don’t think so.’로 동의하거나 반대할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What do you think about ___?’로 상대의 생각을 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I think ___.’로 내 생각을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘I think so, too. / I don’t think so.’로 동의하거나 반대할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

lessons.title: 축하와 위로
lessons.goal: 좋은 소식에 축하하고 나쁜 소식에 위로하기

steps.title: 축하와 위로
steps.goal: 좋은 소식에 축하하고 나쁜 소식에 위로하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 금요일 저녁, 따뜻한 동네 카페 창가 자리. 마야가 활짝 웃으며 휴대폰 속 트로피 사진을 보여 주고, 지우가 박수를 침. 창밖에는 함박눈이 내림
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Congratulations!" (축하와 위로). Goal: 좋은 소식에 축하하고 나쁜 소식에 위로하기. Today's scene: 12월 금요일 저녁, 따뜻한 동네 카페 창가 자리. 마야가 활짝 웃으며 휴대폰 속 트로피 사진을 보여 주고, 지우가 박수를 침. 창밖에는 함박눈이 내림. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.".

steps.en: Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.
steps.when: 좋은 소식을 들었을 때 써요. Congratulations는 늘 끝에 *-s*.
steps.extra: I passed the exam! — Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Congratulations! I’m so happy for you." (축하해요! 정말 잘됐어요.). When to use it: 좋은 소식을 들었을 때 써요. Congratulations는 늘 끝에 -s. Note: I passed the exam! — Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.".

steps.en: That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.
steps.when: 나쁜 소식을 들었을 때 써요. 여기서 sorry는 사과가 아니라 ‘안타까워요’.
steps.extra: I lost my phone. — That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that." (안됐네요. 마음이 안 좋아요.). When to use it: 나쁜 소식을 들었을 때 써요. 여기서 sorry는 사과가 아니라 ‘안타까워요’. Note: I lost my phone. — That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Guess what? ___!".

steps.when: 새 소식을 꺼낼 때 써요. 듣는 사람은 “What?” 하고 받아요.
steps.extra: Guess what? I got a promotion!
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "Guess what? ___!" (있잖아요, ~!). When to use it: 새 소식을 꺼낼 때 써요. 듣는 사람은 “What?” 하고 받아요. Note: Guess what? I got a promotion!
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Good News, Bad News · 금요일 저녁, 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Good News, Bad News · 금요일 저녁, 카페에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, over here! {{Guess what}}? Our team won the company prize!
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 여기요! 있잖아요, 우리 팀이 회사 상을 받았어요!

lines.en: Really? That’s great news! {{Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.}}
lines.ko: 정말요? 좋은 소식이네요! 축하해요! 정말 잘됐어요.

lines.en: Thanks! Ten teams were in the contest, and our app was the winner.

frame: Congratulations! / That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.
head: 소식 (Guess what? …)
이렇게 반응해요
rows: Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.
Good for you! You deserve it.
I’m sorry to hear that. Cheer up!
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Guess what? ___! / Congratulations! / That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that. Table (소식 (Guess what? …) → 이렇게 반응해요):
- I passed my exam! → Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.
- I got a promotion! → Good for you! You deserve it.
- I lost my wallet. → Oh no! That’s too bad.
- I failed my driving test. → I’m sorry to hear that. Cheer up!
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
소식을 듣고 짧게 반응해요.
좋은 소식: *That’s* great! · *That’s* great news!
나쁜 소식: *That’s* too bad. · *That’s* terrible.
happy for · proud of · sorry to

I’m happy *for* you. (네 일이라서) 기뻐요.
I’m proud *of* you. 네가 자랑스러워요.
I’m sorry *to* hear that. 그 말을 들으니 안타까워요.
errors: 이 위로 표현에서는 sorry to hear that을 써요.
deserve 뒤에는 받을 것(it, a break 등)을 꼭 써요.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- That’s + 형용사 / 명사: 소식을 듣고 짧게 반응해요. / 좋은 소식: That’s great! · That’s great news! / 나쁜 소식: That’s too bad. · That’s terrible.
- happy for · proud of · sorry to: I’m happy for you. (네 일이라서) 기뻐요. / I’m proud of you. 네가 자랑스러워요. / I’m sorry to hear that. 그 말을 들으니 안타까워요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Congratulation! → Congratulations! (축하 인사는 늘 -s를 붙여요.)
- I’m sorry for hear that. → I’m sorry to hear that. (이 위로 표현에서는 sorry to hear that을 써요.)
- I’m so happy to you. → I’m so happy for you. (‘당신 일로 기뻐요’는 happy for.)
- You deserve. → You deserve it. (deserve 뒤에는 받을 것(it, a break 등)을 꼭 써요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) passed my exam / 축하 → Guess what? I passed my exam! — Congratulations! I’m so happy for you. · 선생님이 소식을 말하면 바로 축하나 위로로 받아요. Items (situation → model answer): passed my exam → 축하 | got a promotion → 축하 | lost my phone → 위로 | failed my driving test → 위로.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

cards: Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.
That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Congratulations!" (축하와 위로); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Congratulations! I’m so happy for you." / "That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that." / "Guess what? ___!". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Let me know if you need anything.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 축하하기: "Good for you!" (잘됐다!, 친근); "Well done!" (잘했어요!, 보통); "You deserve it." (그럴 자격 있어요., 보통); "That’s great news!" (좋은 소식이네요!, 보통)
- 소식 묻기·반응하기: "Oh no, what happened?" (어머, 무슨 일이에요?, 보통); "That’s terrible." (정말 안됐어요., 보통)
- 위로하기: "I hope things get better." (상황이 나아지면 좋겠어요., 정중); "Cheer up!" (힘내요!, 친근); "Let me know if you need anything." (필요한 거 있으면 말해요., 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 축하할 일 더 보기: get engaged 약혼하다 · get a promotion 승진하다 / pass an exam 시험에 붙다 · win the championship 대회에서 우승하다 / Our team won the championship! 우리 팀이 우승했어요!

Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: ___ what? I passed my exam! B: Congratulations! I’m so happy ___ you. / A: I lost my phone. B: Oh no! I’m sorry to ___ that. ___ up! / 낱말 상자: Guess · for · hear · Cheer
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: congratulations (축하해요), news (소식, 뉴스), proud (자랑스러운), exam (시험), pass ((시험에) 붙다), fail ((시험에) 떨어지다), promotion (승진), engaged (약혼한), cheer (응원하다), lose (잃어버리다; 지다), prize (상, 상품), winner (우승자, 1등).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: deserve (~할 자격이 있다) — "You deserve it."; hope (바라다) — "I hope things get better."; guess (짐작하다) — "Guess what?"; happen ((일이) 일어나다) — "What happened?"; terrible (끔찍한, 아주 나쁜) — "That’s terrible."; sorry (안타까운; 미안한) — "I’m sorry to hear that."; contest (대회) — "a photo contest"; champion (챔피언, 우승자) — "She’s the tennis champion."; disease (병, 질병) — "a skin disease"; suffer ((아픔을) 겪다, 앓다) — "He suffers from headaches.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: Tell me some good news from this week.
Your friend says, “I passed my exam!” What do you say?
Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.
Your friend says, “I lost my phone.” What do you say?
Oh no! That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.
How do you cheer up a friend?
I say, “Cheer up!” / I buy them coffee.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Tell me some good news from this week." (hint on screen: Guess what? I ___!)
- "Your friend says, “I passed my exam!” What do you say?" (hint on screen: Congratulations! I’m so happy for you.)
- "Your friend says, “I lost my phone.” What do you say?" (hint on screen: Oh no! That’s too bad. I’m sorry to hear that.)
- "How do you cheer up a friend?" (hint on screen: I say, “Cheer up!” / I buy them coffee.)
- "When do you feel proud?" (hint on screen: I feel proud when I ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: Tell me some good news from this week.

Your friend says, “I lost my phone.” What do you say?

When do you feel proud?

steps.title: Maya’s Big News
steps.text: Every year, Maya’s company has a *contest* for new ideas. This year, Maya’s team made a health app. Their *previous* app didn’t win, so they worked very hard. It was a simple idea, but *in practice* it took months. This time, they were the winners! The *prize* was a dinner for the whole team. The news went around the office *quickly*. Her boss said, “Well done! You *ought to* be proud.” That evening, Maya cheered Jiwoo up, too. When they left the café, there was snow everywhere. “*Look out* for ice!” said Maya.
steps.gloss: contest 대회 · previous 이전의 · in practice 실제로 해 보면 · prize 상 · quickly 빨리 · ought to ~해야 한다(should와 비슷) · look out 조심하다

steps.title: 어떻게 생겼어요?
steps.goal: 사람의 생김새를 묻고 묘사하기
steps.scene_desc: 12월 토요일 오후, 동네 카페 앞 거리. 휴대폰으로 통화하며 주위를 둘러보는 지우, 길 건너에서 키 크고 안경 쓴 턱수염 남자가 웃으며 손을 흔듦
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What does he look like?" (어떻게 생겼어요?). Goal: 사람의 생김새를 묻고 묘사하기. Today's scene: 12월 토요일 오후, 동네 카페 앞 거리. 휴대폰으로 통화하며 주위를 둘러보는 지우, 길 건너에서 키 크고 안경 쓴 턱수염 남자가 웃으며 손을 흔듦. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What does she look like?".

steps.when: 생김새를 물을 때 써요. 남자면 *he*.
steps.extra: What does he look like? — He’s tall and thin.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What does she look like?" (그 사람 어떻게 생겼어요?). When to use it: 생김새를 물을 때 써요. 남자면 he. Note: What does he look like? — He’s tall and thin.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "She has long ___ hair.".

steps.when: 머리·눈·수염은 *has*로 말해요. 길이 → 모양 → 색 순서.
steps.extra: She has long straight hair. · He has short curly hair.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "She has long ___ hair." (긴 ~ 머리예요.). When to use it: 머리·눈·수염은 has로 말해요. 길이 → 모양 → 색 순서. Note: She has long straight hair. · He has short curly hair.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "He looks like his ___.".

steps.when: 누구와 닮았는지 말할 때 써요. like 뒤에 사람.
steps.extra: He looks like his dad. · She looks like her mom.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "He looks like his ___." (~를 닮았어요.). When to use it: 누구와 닮았는지 말할 때 써요. like 뒤에 사람. Note: He looks like his dad. · She looks like her mom.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Meeting Sam · 토요일 오후, 카페 앞에서 (전화)") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Meeting Sam · 토요일 오후, 카페 앞에서 (전화)

lines.en: Hi, Jiwoo! Thanks for meeting my brother. My class finishes at three.
lines.ko: 안녕하세요, 지우 씨! 제 동생 만나 줘서 고마워요. 수업은 세 시에 끝나요.

lines.en: No problem. But how can I recognize him? {{What does he look like}}?
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 그런데 어떻게 알아보죠? 어떻게 생겼어요?

lines.en: He’s tall and thin. He {{has}} short curly {{hair}}.
lines.ko: 키가 크고 말랐어요. 짧은 곱슬머리예요.

lines.en: Okay. Does he wear glasses?
lines.ko: 알겠어요. 안경 써요?

lines.en: Yes, he wears glasses. And he has a beard.
lines.ko: 네, 안경 써요. 그리고 턱수염이 있어요.

lines.en: Hmm. I see two tall men with beards. Which one is he?
lines.ko: 음. 턱수염 난 키 큰 남자가 두 명 보여요. 어느 쪽이에요?

lines.en: Look at the faces. Sam {{looks like his}} dad. And I look like my dad, too!
lines.ko: 얼굴을 보세요. 샘은 아빠를 닮았어요. 그리고 저도 아빠를 닮았죠!

lines.en: Ha! So you two look alike.
lines.ko: 하하! 그럼 두 사람이 닮았네요.

lines.en: Yep. And he has a nice smile, just like me.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 그리고 웃는 얼굴이 좋아요, 저처럼요.

lines.en: Oh, I see him! He’s waving at me. He’s wearing a dark red scarf.
lines.ko: 아, 보여요! 저한테 손을 흔들어요. 짙은 빨간색 목도리를 했어요.

lines.en: That’s Sam! I told him about your purple sweater.
lines.ko: 샘 맞아요! 지우 씨 보라색 스웨터 이야기를 해 뒀거든요.

lines.en: Great. See you at three, Ben!
lines.ko: 좋아요. 세 시에 봐요, 벤!

Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

frame: He’s ___. He has ___ hair. He looks like his ___.
head: 키·몸 (He’s …)
머리 (She has … hair)
그 밖에
rows: about my height 나와 비슷한 키

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What does he/she look like? / He’s ___. He has ___ hair. He looks like his ___. Table (키·몸 (He’s …) → 머리 (She has … hair)):
- tall 키가 큰 → long straight hair 긴 생머리
- short 키가 작은 → short curly hair 짧은 곱슬머리
- thin 마른 → gray hair 회색 머리, 흰머리
- about my height 나와 비슷한 키 → short black hair 짧은 검은 머리
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
키·몸은 *be*: He*’s* tall. She*’s* thin.
머리·눈·수염은 *have*: He *has* a beard. She *has* brown eyes.

He *looks like* his dad. 아빠를 닮았어요. (like + 사람)
She *looks* young. 젊어 보여요. (look + 형용사)
errors: 남자는 he. 말할 때 he와 she를 자주 섞어 써요.
머리카락 전체를 말할 땐 a 없이.
look like 뒤에는 사람, 형용사는 look 바로 뒤에.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- be 와 have: 키·몸은 be: He’s tall. She’s thin. / 머리·눈·수염은 have: He has a beard. She has brown eyes.
- look like · look: He looks like his dad. 아빠를 닮았어요. (like + 사람) / She looks young. 젊어 보여요. (look + 형용사)
Common mistakes on screen:
- He is glasses. → He wears glasses. (안경은 wear(쓰다).)
- Sam? She has a beard. → Sam? He has a beard. (남자는 he. 말할 때 he와 she를 자주 섞어 써요.)
- She has a long hair. → She has long hair. (머리카락 전체를 말할 땐 a 없이.)
- He looks like tall. → He looks tall. (look like 뒤에는 사람, 형용사는 look 바로 뒤에.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.

look like · look: He looks like his dad. 아빠를 닮았어요. (like + 사람)She looks young. 젊어 보여요. (look + 형용사)
mistakes: He is glasses. → He wears glasses.
Sam? She has a beard. → Sam? He has a beard.
She has a long hair. → She has long hair.
He looks like tall. → He looks tall.

steps.note: 예) tall / short curly hair → He’s tall. He has short curly hair. · 선생님이 그림 사전 속 사람을 고르면 바로 묘사해요.
steps.teach:

Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What does she look like?" / "She has long ___ hair." / "He looks like his ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. steps.title: Sam’s Visit
steps.text: Ben’s brother Sam came from Boston for a week. Jiwoo met him at a café. She didn’t know what he looked like, but Ben described his *appearance* — tall, glasses, a beard, *and so on*. So it was easy to identify him. Sam is nearly two meters tall, so he *looks down* at most people! He has a little gray in his beard. He is a nurse, and he *looks after* sick children. *In the long term*, he wants to work in Seoul. Before he left, he took a photo of himself with Ben and Jiwoo. “I’ll *look back* on this day and smile,” he said.
steps.gloss: appearance 생김새 · and so on 기타 등등 · identify 알아보다 · nearly 거의 · look down 내려다보다 · look after 돌보다 · in the long term 나중에는 · himself 그 자신 · look back (on) 돌아보다
questions: How tall is Sam?
What does Sam do in Boston?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Sam’s Visit". Text: "Ben’s brother Sam came from Boston for a week. Jiwoo met him at a café. She didn’t know what he looked like, but Ben described his appearance — tall, glasses, a beard, and so on. So it was easy to identify him. Sam is nearly two meters tall, so he looks down at most people! He has a little gray in his beard. He is a nurse, and he looks after sick children. In the long term, he wants to work in Seoul. Before he left, he took a photo of himself with Ben and Jiwoo. “I’ll look back on this day and smile,” he said." Words: appearance 생김새 · and so on 기타 등등 · identify 알아보다 · nearly 거의 · look down 내려다보다 · look after 돌보다 · in the long term 나중에는 · himself 그 자신 · look back (on) 돌아보다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "How tall is Sam?" / "What does Sam do in Boston?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

steps.title: 부탁하기
steps.goal: 공손하게 부탁하고, 들어주고, 고마워하기
steps.scene_desc: 1월 아침, 아파트 5층 복도. 작은 여행 가방을 든 지우가 옆집 그레이스에게 열쇠를 건네고, 지우 집 문 안쪽으로 화분 몇 개가 보임
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Could you water my plants?" (부탁하기). Goal: 공손하게 부탁하고, 들어주고, 고마워하기. Today's scene: 1월 아침, 아파트 5층 복도. 작은 여행 가방을 든 지우가 옆집 그레이스에게 열쇠를 건네고, 지우 집 문 안쪽으로 화분 몇 개가 보임. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Could you ___, please?".

steps.when: 공손하게 부탁할 때 써요. Can you ~?보다 부드러워요.
steps.extra: Could you water my plants, please?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Could you ___, please?" (~해 주시겠어요?). When to use it: 공손하게 부탁할 때 써요. Can you ~?보다 부드러워요. Note: Could you water my plants, please?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Sure, no problem.".

steps.when: 부탁을 기꺼이 들어줄 때 써요.
steps.extra: Could you open the window? — Sure, no problem.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Sure, no problem." (그럼요, 문제없어요.). When to use it: 부탁을 기꺼이 들어줄 때 써요. Note: Could you open the window? — Sure, no problem.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Thanks a lot. I owe you one.".

steps.en: Thanks a lot. I owe you one.
steps.when: 도움을 받고 고마움을 표현해요. I owe you one = 다음에 꼭 갚을게요.
steps.extra: 대답: Anytime. (언제든지요)
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "Thanks a lot. I owe you one." (정말 고마워요. 신세 졌어요.). When to use it: 도움을 받고 고마움을 표현해요. I owe you one = 다음에 꼭 갚을게요. Note: 대답: Anytime. (언제든지요).
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

10. Grace: "Don’t worry about your plants. Just enjoy Busan!" (화분은 걱정 말아요. 부산 잘 다녀와요!)

12. Grace: "Anytime." (언제든지요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.

5. Jiwoo (learner): "Could you water my plants on Thursday, please? I don’t know anybody else on this floor." (목요일에 화분에 물 좀 주시겠어요? 이 층에는 그레이스 말고 아는 사람이 없어서요.)
6. Grace (you): "Sure, no problem. Shall I get your packages, too?" (그럼요, 문제없어요. 택배도 받아 둘까요?)
7. Jiwoo (learner): "Yes, please! A box is coming on Friday. Oh, would you hold this for a second?" (네, 부탁해요! 금요일에 상자가 하나 와요. 앗, 이것 좀 잠깐 들어 줄래요?)

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Grace. The learner speaks first: call highlight_line with 1 and invite them to start. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

6. Grace: "Sure, no problem. Shall I get your packages, too?" (그럼요, 문제없어요. 택배도 받아 둘까요?)
7. Jiwoo: "Yes, please! A box is coming on Friday. Oh, would you hold this for a second?" (네, 부탁해요! 금요일에 상자가 하나 와요. 앗, 이것 좀 잠깐 들어 줄래요?)

9. Jiwoo: "Here’s my spare key. That’s very kind of you, Grace." (여기 여분 열쇠예요. 정말 친절하시네요, 그레이스.)

Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: Sure, no problem. / Thanks a lot. I owe you one.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Could you ___, please? / Sure, no problem. / Thanks a lot. I owe you one. Table (부탁할 일 → 이렇게 부탁해요):
- water my plants 화분에 물 주다 → Could you water my plants, please?
- get my packages 택배를 받다 → Could you get my packages, please?
- lend me an umbrella 우산을 빌려주다 → Could you lend me an umbrella, please?

Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
부탁을 공손하게: *Could you* open the window, please?
대답: Sure. / Of course. 거절: Sorry, I can’t right now.

*lend* 빌려주다(내 것을 남에게): Could you *lend* me your pen?
*borrow* 빌리다(남의 것을 내가): Can I *borrow* your pen?
방향이 반대예요.
errors: Could you borrow me your pen?
Could you lend me your pen?
Could you to water my plants?

Can you make me a favor?

me·it 같은 말은 pick과 up 사이에.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- Could you + 동사원형 ~?: 부탁을 공손하게: Could you open the window, please? / 대답: Sure. / Of course. 거절: Sorry, I can’t right now.
- lend 와 borrow: lend 빌려주다(내 것을 남에게): Could you lend me your pen? / borrow 빌리다(남의 것을 내가): Can I borrow your pen? / 방향이 반대예요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Could you borrow me your pen? → Could you lend me your pen? (빌려주는 건 lend. borrow는 ‘내가 빌리다’예요.)
- Could you to water my plants? → Could you water my plants? (Could you 뒤엔 to 없이 동사원형.)
- Can you make me a favor? → Can you do me a favor? (favor는 do와 함께 써요.)
- Could you pick up me? → Could you pick me up? (me·it 같은 말은 pick과 up 사이에.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) open / the window → Could you open the window, please? — Sure, no problem. Items (situation → model answer): open → the window | lend me → your pen | carry → this bag | copy → this file.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). cards: Thanks a lot. I owe you one.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Could you water my plants?" (부탁하기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Could you ___, please?" / "Sure, no problem." / "Thanks a lot. I owe you one.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Can you do me a favor?
Could you give me a hand?
Would you hold this for a second?
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 부탁 꺼내기: "Can you do me a favor?" (부탁 하나 해도 돼요?, 친근); "Could you give me a hand?" (좀 도와주시겠어요?, 보통); "Could you pick me up?" (저 좀 데리러 와 줄래요?, 친근); "Would you hold this for a second?" (이것 좀 잠깐 들어 줄래요?, 보통)
- 들어주기·거절하기: "Of course." (물론이죠., 보통); "I’d be happy to." (기꺼이요., 정중); "Sorry, I can’t right now." (미안해요, 지금은 안 돼요., 보통)
- 고마워하기: "That’s very kind of you." (정말 친절하시네요., 정중); "Anytime." (언제든지요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Picture words on screen. New: hand (손; (a hand) 도움), pick (집다, 고르다), carry (들고 가다, 나르다), lend (빌려주다), borrow (빌리다), copy (복사(하다)), document (서류), file (파일, 서류철), hold (들고 있다, 잡다), open (열다), close (닫다), package (택배, 소포).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Three Days in Busan
steps.text: Last week, Jiwoo went to Busan for three days. She *carried out* a big design project with a team there. She took a lot of documents in a big file. Grace, *on the other hand*, stayed in Seoul. She watered Jiwoo’s plants and took in her package. Then she sent a photo: “Your plants look happy. *Carry on* with your work!” On Friday, snow *held up* Jiwoo’s train. *At the time*, she was very tired, but she smiled. At home, she opened the box. In it, there was a small object: a new desk lamp. Then she knocked on Grace’s door with some snacks from Busan. “I owe you one!”
steps.gloss: carry out (일을) 해내다 · on the other hand 한편 · take in 받아 두다 · carry on 계속하다 · hold up 늦어지게 하다 · at the time 그때(당시) · object 물건
questions: What did Grace do for Jiwoo?
What held up Jiwoo’s train?

Carry on with your work!” On Friday, snow held up Jiwoo’s train. At the time, she was very tired, but she smiled. At home, she opened the box. In it, there was a small object: a new desk lamp. Then she knocked on Grace’s door with some snacks from Busan. “I owe you one!”" Words: carry out (일을) 해내다 · on the other hand 한편 · take in 받아 두다 · carry on 계속하다 · hold up 늦어지게 하다 · at the time 그때(당시) · object 물건.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did Grace do for Jiwoo?" / "What held up Jiwoo’s train?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 도와줄게요
steps.goal: 도움을 제안하고 받아들이거나 사양하기
steps.scene_desc: 1월 토요일 오후, 아파트 5층 그레이스네 현관 앞. 커다랗고 납작한 책장 상자를 그레이스가 끌고 있고, 지우가 다가와 손을 내밂
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Do you need a hand?" (도와줄게요). Goal: 도움을 제안하고 받아들이거나 사양하기. Today's scene: 1월 토요일 오후, 아파트 5층 그레이스네 현관 앞. 커다랗고 납작한 책장 상자를 그레이스가 끌고 있고, 지우가 다가와 손을 내밂. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Do you need a hand?".

steps.when: 힘들어 보이는 사람에게 도움을 제안해요. a hand = 도움의 손.
steps.extra: 대답: That would be great. / Thanks, but I’m fine.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Do you need a hand?" (도와줄까요?). When to use it: 힘들어 보이는 사람에게 도움을 제안해요. a hand = 도움의 손. Note: 대답: That would be great. / Thanks, but I’m fine.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’ll help you.".

steps.when: 그 자리에서 바로 ‘할게요’라고 할 때 I’ll(= I will).
steps.extra: I’ll carry it. · I’ll take care of it.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I’ll help you." (제가 도와줄게요.). When to use it: 그 자리에서 바로 ‘할게요’라고 할 때 I’ll(= I will). Note: I’ll carry it. · I’ll take care of it.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Let me ___.".

steps.when: 내가 하겠다고 나설 때 써요. Let me 뒤엔 동사원형.
steps.extra: Let me read the instructions. · Let me get that for you.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "Let me ___." (제가 ~할게요.). When to use it: 내가 하겠다고 나설 때 써요. Let me 뒤엔 동사원형. Note: Let me read the instructions. · Let me get that for you.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("The New Bookshelf · 1월 토요일, 그레이스네 집 앞에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Do you need a hand? / Let me ___. / That would be great. / Thanks, but I’m fine. Table (이럴 때 → 이렇게 도와요):
- heavy box 무거운 상자 → Let me carry it. / I’ll carry it.
- closed door 닫힌 문 → Let me get that for you.
- broken chair 망가진 의자 → Let me fix it.
- busy friend 바쁜 친구 → Leave it to me. I’ll take care of it.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 제안하는 I’ll: 그 자리에서 ‘제가 할게요’: I’ll help you. I’ll carry it. / I’ll = I will. / 미리 정한 계획은 be going to: I’m going to visit Busan.
- Let me + 동사원형: 내가 하겠다고 나설 때: Let me read it. 제가 읽을게요. / Let me get that for you. 제가 해 드릴게요. / Let me 뒤에 to·-ing를 붙이지 않아요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Let me to help you. → Let me help you. (Let me 뒤엔 to 없이 동사원형.)
- Do you need a hands? → Do you need a hand? (a 뒤에는 하나: a hand.)
- I’ll carry. → I’ll carry it. (carry 뒤엔 무엇을(it)을 꼭 넣어요.)
- I’ll take care it. → I’ll take care of it. (take care 뒤에 of를 빼지 않아요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.

steps.title: Grace’s Bookshelf
steps.text: On Saturday, Grace’s new bookshelf came in a big, heavy box. Jiwoo helped her *take off* the plastic. Grace *takes on* a lot of work every week, so she was tired. After an hour, Jiwoo said, “Let me *take over*.” Grace directed, and Jiwoo did the hard parts. By evening, the bookshelf was complete. It *takes up* a whole wall, plus it has room for two hundred books! Grace also volunteers at a small library on Sundays. Next week, Jiwoo is going to go with her.
steps.gloss: take off 떼다, 벗기다 · take on (일을) 맡다 · take over 이어서 하다, 넘겨받다 · direct 지시하다 · complete 다 된, 완성된 · take up (자리를) 차지하다 · plus 게다가 · room 공간
questions: Why was Grace tired?
What does Grace do on Sundays?

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "You don’t have to bring anything." (해야 해요). Goal: 해야 하는 일과 안 해도 되는 일 말하기. Today's scene: 1월 평일 저녁, 아파트 엘리베이터 안. 노트북 가방을 멘 지친 지우와 장바구니를 든 벤이 이야기하고, 엘리베이터 문이 3층 복도 쪽으로 열림. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I have to ___.".

steps.when: 일·일정·약속 때문에 꼭 해야 하는 일을 말해요.

steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I have to ___." (~해야 해요.). When to use it: 일·일정·약속 때문에 꼭 해야 하는 일을 말해요. Note: I have to finish my report by Friday.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Do you have to ___?".

steps.when: 상대가 꼭 해야 하는지 물어요.

steps.when: 꼭 하지 않아도 된다고 말해요. ‘하면 안 돼요’가 아니에요.

steps.teach:
