steps.title: The New Year Party · 저녁, 엘리베이터에서

lines.en: Hi, Jiwoo! You look tired. Long day?
lines.ko: 안녕, 지우! 피곤해 보이네요. 힘든 하루였어요?

lines.en: Yes. I must finish my current project by Friday.
lines.ko: 네. 지금 하는 프로젝트를 금요일까지 꼭 끝내야 해요.

lines.en: Here’s how people really say it: “I have to finish it.” “Must” sounds very strong.
lines.ko: 사람들은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “I have to finish it.” must는 아주 강하게 들려요.

lines.en: Okay. {{I have to}} finish it by Friday. So far, so good.
lines.ko: 알겠어요. 금요일까지 끝내야 해요. 지금까지는 괜찮아요.

lines.en: Good. Hey, I’m having a New Year potluck on Friday evening. Can you come?
lines.ko: 잘됐네요. 참, 금요일 저녁에 새해 포틀럭 모임을 해요. 올 수 있어요?

lines.en: Friday? I have to work till six. What time does it start?
lines.ko: 금요일이요? 6시까지 일해야 해요. 몇 시에 시작해요?

lines.en: At seven-thirty. But it ends early.
lines.ko: 7시 반이요. 그래도 일찍 끝나요.

lines.en: {{Do you have to}} get up early on Saturday?
lines.ko: 토요일에 일찍 일어나야 해요?

lines.en: Yes. I have to prepare for my morning class.
lines.ko: 네. 아침 수업 준비를 해야 해요.

lines.en: Then I can come! But it’s a potluck. Do I have to bring anything?
lines.ko: 그럼 갈 수 있어요! 그런데 포틀럭이잖아요. 뭐 가져가야 해요?

lines.en: No, {{you don’t have to}}. You’re busy this week. Just come.
lines.ko: 아뇨, 안 그래도 돼요. 이번 주 바쁘잖아요. 그냥 와요.

lines.en: Really? That’s a relief! Thanks, Ben.
lines.ko: 정말요? 다행이에요! 고마워요, 벤.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The New Year Party · 저녁, 엘리베이터에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Ben: "Hi, Jiwoo! You look tired. Long day?" (안녕, 지우! 피곤해 보이네요. 힘든 하루였어요?)

3. Ben: "Here’s how people really say it: “I have to finish it.” “Must” sounds very strong." (사람들은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “I have to finish it.” must는 아주 강하게 들려요.)
4. Jiwoo: "Okay. I have to finish it by Friday. So far, so good." (알겠어요. 금요일까지 끝내야 해요. 지금까지는 괜찮아요.)
5. Ben: "Good. Hey, I’m having a New Year potluck on Friday evening. Can you come?" (잘됐네요. 참, 금요일 저녁에 새해 포틀럭 모임을 해요. 올 수 있어요?)
6. Jiwoo: "Friday? I have to work till six. What time does it start?" (금요일이요? 6시까지 일해야 해요. 몇 시에 시작해요?)
7. Ben: "At seven-thirty. But it ends early." (7시 반이요. 그래도 일찍 끝나요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Do you have to get up early on Saturday?" (토요일에 일찍 일어나야 해요?)
9. Ben: "Yes. I have to prepare for my morning class." (네. 아침 수업 준비를 해야 해요.)
10. Jiwoo: "Then I can come! But it’s a potluck. Do I have to bring anything?" (그럼 갈 수 있어요! 그런데 포틀럭이잖아요. 뭐 가져가야 해요?)
11. Ben: "No, you don’t have to. You’re busy this week. Just come." (아뇨, 안 그래도 돼요. 이번 주 바쁘잖아요. 그냥 와요.)
12. Jiwoo: "Really? That’s a relief! Thanks, Ben." (정말요? 다행이에요! 고마워요, 벤.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

frame: I have to ___. / Do you have to ___?
You don’t have to ___. / No, you don’t have to.
head: 해야 해요 (have to)
안 해도 돼요 (don’t have to)
rows: I *have to* get up early tomorrow.
She *doesn’t have to* work on Saturday.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: I have to ___. / Do you have to ___? / You don’t have to ___. / No, you don’t have to. Table (해야 해요 (have to) → 안 해도 돼요 (don’t have to)):
- I have to work late tonight. → You don’t have to come early.
- I have to get up early tomorrow. → You don’t have to bring anything.
- She has to finish a report. → She doesn’t have to work on Saturday.
- Do you have to wait? → No, I don’t have to.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
I *have to* go. 가야 해요.
he·she는 *has to*: Ben *has to* work.
지난 일은 *had to*: I *had to* wait.
don’t have to = 안 해도 돼요

꼭 할 필요는 없어요. ‘하면 안 돼요’가 아니에요.
물을 때: *Do* I *have to* come?
대답: No, you *don’t have to*.
errors: I have to finishing my report.
I have to finish my report.
She have to get up early.
She has to get up early.
must 뒤에는 to 없이 바로 동사.
You don’t have to bring nothing.
You don’t have to bring anything.
don’t와 nothing을 같이 쓰지 않아요. don’t 뒤에는 anything.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- have to + 동사원형: I have to go. 가야 해요. / he·she는 has to: Ben has to work. / 지난 일은 had to: I had to wait.
- don’t have to = 안 해도 돼요: 꼭 할 필요는 없어요. ‘하면 안 돼요’가 아니에요. / 물을 때: Do I have to come? / 대답: No, you don’t have to.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I have to finishing my report. → I have to finish my report. (have to 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- She have to get up early. → She has to get up early. (she·he 뒤에는 has to.)
- I must to go now. → I must go now. (must 뒤에는 to 없이 바로 동사.)
- You don’t have to bring nothing. → You don’t have to bring anything. (don’t와 nothing을 같이 쓰지 않아요. don’t 뒤에는 anything.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) finish a report / come early → I have to finish a report, but I don’t have to come early.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) finish a report / come early → I have to finish a report, but I don’t have to come early. Items (situation → model answer): finish a report → come early | get up early → cook dinner | prepare for a meeting → wear a suit | do my homework → clean the house.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "You don’t have to bring anything." (해야 해요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I have to ___." / "Do you have to ___?" / "You don’t have to ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I have to work late tonight.
I have to get up early tomorrow.
I had to wait for an hour.
I really have to go now.
Do I have to bring anything?
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 해야 할 일 말하기: "I have to work late tonight." (오늘 밤 늦게까지 일해야 해요., 보통); "I have to get up early tomorrow." (내일 일찍 일어나야 해요., 보통); "I had to wait for an hour." (한 시간이나 기다려야 했어요., 보통); "I really have to go now." (이제 정말 가 봐야 해요., 친근)
- 꼭 해야 하는지 묻고 답하기: "Do I have to bring anything?" (뭐 가져가야 해요?, 보통); "No, you don’t have to." (아뇨, 안 그래도 돼요., 보통); "It’s not necessary." (그럴 필요 없어요., 정중)
- 규칙·안심: "You must wear a seatbelt." (안전벨트를 꼭 매야 해요., 정중); "That’s a relief." (다행이에요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: have to · must · ought to

*have to* 해야 해요 — 말할 때 가장 많이 써요.
*must* 꼭 해야 해요 — 규칙·안내문 느낌: You must wear a seatbelt.
*must not* 하면 안 돼요 ≠ don’t have to
(참고) You *ought* to rest. 쉬는 게 좋겠어요.
규칙에 쓰는 말

It’s a *rule*. 규칙이에요.
No pets *allowed*. 반려동물 금지
a parking *permit* 주차 허가증
It’s not *necessary*. 그럴 필요 없어요.
steps.blank:
A: Do I ___ to bring anything?   B: No, you don’t ___ to. Just come.
A: Really? That’s a ___!   B: See you on Friday. I really have to ___ now.
낱말 상자: have · have · relief · go
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- have to · must · ought to: have to 해야 해요 — 말할 때 가장 많이 써요. / must 꼭 해야 해요 — 규칙·안내문 느낌: You must wear a seatbelt. / must not 하면 안 돼요 ≠ don’t have to / (참고) You ought to rest. 쉬는 게 좋겠어요.
- 규칙에 쓰는 말: It’s a rule. 규칙이에요. / No pets allowed. 반려동물 금지 / a parking permit 주차 허가증 / It’s not necessary. 그럴 필요 없어요.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Do I ___ to bring anything? B: No, you don’t ___ to. Just come. / A: Really? That’s a ___! B: See you on Friday. I really have to ___ now. / 낱말 상자: have · have · relief · go
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: seatbelt (안전벨트), report (보고서), homework (숙제), deadline (마감), meeting (회의), wait (기다리다), hour (한 시간), tonight (오늘 밤), early (일찍), late (늦게), organize (정리하다), prepare (준비하다).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: must (꼭 ~해야 하다) — "You must wear a seatbelt."; necessary (필요한) — "It’s not necessary."; relief (안심, 다행) — "That’s a relief."; rule (규칙) — "It’s a rule."; allowed (허락된) — "Pets are not allowed here."; finish (끝내다) — "finish a project"; permit (허가증; 허락하다) — "a parking permit"; preparation (준비) — "class preparation"; current (지금의, 현재의) — "my current project"; till (~까지(= until)) — "I work till six.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What do you have to do tomorrow?
Do you have to get up early on weekdays?
Yes, I have to get up at ___. / No, I don’t have to.
What don’t you have to do on weekends?
On weekends, I don’t have to ___.
A friend invites you to a potluck. What do you ask?
Do I have to bring anything?
Your friend says, “You don’t have to.” How do you feel?
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What do you have to do tomorrow?" (hint on screen: I have to ___.)
- "Do you have to get up early on weekdays?" (hint on screen: Yes, I have to get up at ___. / No, I don’t have to.)
- "What don’t you have to do on weekends?" (hint on screen: On weekends, I don’t have to ___.)
- "A friend invites you to a potluck. What do you ask?" (hint on screen: Do I have to bring anything?)
- "Your friend says, “You don’t have to.” How do you feel?" (hint on screen: That’s a relief! / Great, thanks!)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s Busy Week
steps.text: This week, Jiwoo has a big deadline. She has to finish a new web page by Friday at six. The project *takes up* all her time. At the Monday meeting, her team leader *brings up* the deadline again. *So far*, everything is going well. Jiwoo just has to *focus on* her work and organize her time. She doesn’t have to work on the weekend. And on Friday evening, she is going to Ben’s New Year potluck. Everyone brings food, but Jiwoo doesn’t have to. What a relief!
steps.gloss: take up (시간·자리를) 차지하다 · bring up (이야기를) 꺼내다 · so far 지금까지 · focus on ~에 집중하다 · potluck 각자 음식을 가져오는 모임
questions: What does Jiwoo have to finish?
Does Jiwoo have to bring food to the party?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Jiwoo’s Busy Week". Text: "This week, Jiwoo has a big deadline. She has to finish a new web page by Friday at six. The project takes up all her time. At the Monday meeting, her team leader brings up the deadline again. So far, everything is going well. Jiwoo just has to focus on her work and organize her time. She doesn’t have to work on the weekend. And on Friday evening, she is going to Ben’s New Year potluck. Everyone brings food, but Jiwoo doesn’t have to. What a relief!" Words: take up (시간·자리를) 차지하다 · bring up (이야기를) 꺼내다 · so far 지금까지 · focus on ~에 집중하다 · potluck 각자 음식을 가져오는 모임.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What does Jiwoo have to finish?" / "Does Jiwoo have to bring food to the party?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘I have to ___.’로 해야 하는 일을 말할 수 있어요.
‘Do you have to ___?’로 꼭 해야 하는지 물을 수 있어요.
‘You don’t have to ___.’로 안 해도 된다고 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘I have to ___.’로 해야 하는 일을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘Do you have to ___?’로 꼭 해야 하는지 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘You don’t have to ___.’로 안 해도 된다고 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

lessons.title: 약속 바꾸기
lessons.goal: 약속을 바꾸자고 하고 다른 날을 제안하거나 거절하기

steps.title: 약속 바꾸기
steps.goal: 약속을 바꾸자고 하고 다른 날을 제안하거나 거절하기
steps.scene_desc: 1월 저녁, 화면이 둘로 나뉨. 왼쪽은 회사 책상에서 휴대폰으로 통화하며 탁상 달력을 보는 지우, 오른쪽은 집 거실 소파 옆에 스케이트를 두고 통화하는 벤(글자는 보이지 않게)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "How about Sunday instead?" (약속 바꾸기). Goal: 약속을 바꾸자고 하고 다른 날을 제안하거나 거절하기. Today's scene: 1월 저녁, 화면이 둘로 나뉨. 왼쪽은 회사 책상에서 휴대폰으로 통화하며 탁상 달력을 보는 지우, 오른쪽은 집 거실 소파 옆에 스케이트를 두고 통화하는 벤(글자는 보이지 않게). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Can we change our plan?".

steps.when: 친구와 정한 약속을 바꾸자고 할 때 써요. 앞에 미안하다는 말을 붙이면 더 부드러워요.
steps.extra: I’m so sorry. Can we change our plan?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Can we change our plan?" (약속을 바꿀 수 있을까요?). When to use it: 친구와 정한 약속을 바꾸자고 할 때 써요. 앞에 미안하다는 말을 붙이면 더 부드러워요. Note: I’m so sorry. Can we change our plan?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "How about ___ instead?".

steps.when: 원래 날·시간·장소 대신 다른 것을 제안해요.
steps.extra: How about Sunday instead?
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "How about ___ instead?" (대신 ~는 어때요?). When to use it: 원래 날·시간·장소 대신 다른 것을 제안해요. Note: How about Sunday instead?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That works for me.".

steps.when: 제안한 날·시간이 나한테 괜찮을 때 써요.
steps.extra: Sunday at two? That works for me.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That works for me." (저는 좋아요.). When to use it: 제안한 날·시간이 나한테 괜찮을 때 써요. Note: Sunday at two? That works for me.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("A Change of Plans · 저녁, 전화로") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: A Change of Plans · 저녁, 전화로

lines.en: Hi, Ben. It’s Jiwoo. Do you have a minute?
lines.ko: 안녕하세요, 벤. 지우예요. 잠깐 통화 괜찮아요?

lines.en: Sure. What’s up?
lines.ko: 그럼요. 무슨 일이에요?

lines.en: I’m so sorry about this, but something came up on Saturday morning.
lines.ko: 정말 미안한데, 토요일 오전에 일이 생겼어요.

lines.en: Oh? What happened?
lines.ko: 그래요? 무슨 일인데요?

lines.en: It has to do with work. Can we postpone our appointment?
lines.ko: 일 때문이에요. 약속을 미룰 수 있을까요?

lines.en: No worries! For a casual outing, I’d just say, “{{Can we change our plan}}?”
lines.ko: 괜찮아요! 친구랑 노는 약속이면 그냥 이렇게 말해요. “Can we change our plan?”

lines.en: Oh! Can we change our plan? {{How about}} Sunday {{instead}}?
lines.ko: 아! 약속을 바꿀 수 있을까요? 대신 일요일은 어때요?

lines.en: Let me check my schedule… I’m available after one. Is two okay with you?
lines.ko: 일정 좀 볼게요… 1시 이후는 괜찮아요. 2시 괜찮아요?

lines.en: Yes! {{That works for me}}.
lines.ko: 네! 저는 좋아요.

lines.en: Great. Let’s skate for an hour or so.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 한 시간쯤 스케이트 타요.

lines.en: Perfect. Thanks for understanding, Ben.
lines.ko: 좋아요. 이해해 줘서 고마워요, 벤.

lines.en: No worries. See you then!
lines.ko: 괜찮아요. 그때 봐요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "A Change of Plans · 저녁, 전화로", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Jiwoo: "Hi, Ben. It’s Jiwoo. Do you have a minute?" (안녕하세요, 벤. 지우예요. 잠깐 통화 괜찮아요?)
2. Ben: "Sure. What’s up?" (그럼요. 무슨 일이에요?)
3. Jiwoo: "I’m so sorry about this, but something came up on Saturday morning." (정말 미안한데, 토요일 오전에 일이 생겼어요.)
4. Ben: "Oh? What happened?" (그래요? 무슨 일인데요?)
5. Jiwoo: "It has to do with work. Can we postpone our appointment?" (일 때문이에요. 약속을 미룰 수 있을까요?)
6. Ben: "No worries! For a casual outing, I’d just say, “Can we change our plan?”" (괜찮아요! 친구랑 노는 약속이면 그냥 이렇게 말해요. “Can we change our plan?”)
7. Jiwoo: "Oh! Can we change our plan? How about Sunday instead?" (아! 약속을 바꿀 수 있을까요? 대신 일요일은 어때요?)
8. Ben: "Let me check my schedule… I’m available after one. Is two okay with you?" (일정 좀 볼게요… 1시 이후는 괜찮아요. 2시 괜찮아요?)
9. Jiwoo: "Yes! That works for me." (네! 저는 좋아요.)
10. Ben: "Great. Let’s skate for an hour or so." (좋아요. 한 시간쯤 스케이트 타요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Perfect. Thanks for understanding, Ben." (좋아요. 이해해 줘서 고마워요, 벤.)
12. Ben: "No worries. See you then!" (괜찮아요. 그때 봐요!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Ben. The learner speaks first: call highlight_line with 1 and invite them to start. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

items: Jiwoo has to work on Saturday morning.
They are going to meet at one.
They are going to skate on Sunday.
steps.teach:
True/false check. The statements on the learner's screen:
1. Jiwoo has to work on Saturday morning.
2. They are going to meet at one.
3. They are going to skate on Sunday.
The scene they are about:
1. Jiwoo: "Hi, Ben. It’s Jiwoo. Do you have a minute?" (안녕하세요, 벤. 지우예요. 잠깐 통화 괜찮아요?)
2. Ben: "Sure. What’s up?" (그럼요. 무슨 일이에요?)
3. Jiwoo: "I’m so sorry about this, but something came up on Saturday morning." (정말 미안한데, 토요일 오전에 일이 생겼어요.)
4. Ben: "Oh? What happened?" (그래요? 무슨 일인데요?)
5. Jiwoo: "It has to do with work. Can we postpone our appointment?" (일 때문이에요. 약속을 미룰 수 있을까요?)
6. Ben: "No worries! For a casual outing, I’d just say, “Can we change our plan?”" (괜찮아요! 친구랑 노는 약속이면 그냥 이렇게 말해요. “Can we change our plan?”)
7. Jiwoo: "Oh! Can we change our plan? How about Sunday instead?" (아! 약속을 바꿀 수 있을까요? 대신 일요일은 어때요?)
8. Ben: "Let me check my schedule… I’m available after one. Is two okay with you?" (일정 좀 볼게요… 1시 이후는 괜찮아요. 2시 괜찮아요?)
9. Jiwoo: "Yes! That works for me." (네! 저는 좋아요.)
10. Ben: "Great. Let’s skate for an hour or so." (좋아요. 한 시간쯤 스케이트 타요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Perfect. Thanks for understanding, Ben." (좋아요. 이해해 줘서 고마워요, 벤.)
12. Ben: "No worries. See you then!" (괜찮아요. 그때 봐요!)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: Can we change our plan? How about ___ instead?
That works for me. / That doesn’t work for me.
head: 제안 (How about …?)
대답
rows: Sorry, that doesn’t work for me.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Can we change our plan? How about ___ instead? / That works for me. / That doesn’t work for me. Table (제안 (How about …?) → 대답):
- How about Sunday instead? → Sunday? That works for me.
- How about two o’clock? → Sorry, that doesn’t work for me.
- How about the café instead? → Sure. See you then.
- How about next week? → Let me check my schedule.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
다른 날·시간·장소를 제안해요.
How about *Sunday*? · How about *two o’clock*?
동사는 *-ing*로: How about *meeting* at two?
끝에 *instead*(대신)를 붙이면 ‘원래 계획 대신’이라는 뜻이에요.

That *works* for me. 저는 좋아요.
That *doesn’t work* for me. 저는 안 돼요.
사람이 아니라 날·시간이 주어예요: Does Sunday *work* for you?
errors: Let’s put off it until next week.
Let’s put it off until next week.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- How about ~?: 다른 날·시간·장소를 제안해요. / How about Sunday? · How about two o’clock? / 동사는 -ing로: How about meeting at two? / 끝에 instead(대신)를 붙이면 ‘원래 계획 대신’이라는 뜻이에요.
- work = (날·시간이) 괜찮다: That works for me. 저는 좋아요. / That doesn’t work for me. 저는 안 돼요. / 사람이 아니라 날·시간이 주어예요: Does Sunday work for you?
Common mistakes on screen:
- How about meet on Sunday? → How about meeting on Sunday? (How about 뒤의 동사는 -ing.)
- That’s work for me. → That works for me. (That 뒤에 is 없이 works.)
- Is Sunday okay to you? → Is Sunday okay with you? (okay 뒤에는 with you.)
- Let’s put off it until next week. → Let’s put it off until next week. (it은 put과 off 사이에.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

That’s work for me. → That works for me.
Is Sunday okay to you? → Is Sunday okay with you?
Let’s put off it until next week. → Let’s put it off until next week.

steps.note: 예) Saturday / Sunday → Can we change our plan? How about Sunday instead?
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) Saturday / Sunday → Can we change our plan? How about Sunday instead? Items (situation → model answer): Saturday → Sunday | ten o’clock → two o’clock | the park → the café | this week → next week.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "How about Sunday instead?" (약속 바꾸기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Can we change our plan?" / "How about ___ instead?" / "That works for me.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: Let’s put it off until next week.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 바꾸자고 하기: "Something came up." (일이 좀 생겼어요., 보통); "I’m so sorry about this." (정말 미안해요., 보통); "Can we make it later?" (좀 늦게 만나도 될까요?, 친근); "Let’s put it off until next week." (다음 주로 미뤄요., 보통)
- 다른 때 정하기: "Is ___ okay with you?" (~ 괜찮아요?, 보통); "Let me check my schedule." (일정 좀 볼게요., 보통)
- 대답하기: "That doesn’t work for me." (저는 그때 안 돼요., 보통); "No worries." (괜찮아요., 친근); "See you then." (그때 봐요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 미루기·취소하기

*postpone* = put off 미루다
*cancel* 취소하다 · The train is *delayed*. 기차가 늦어져요.
Can I take a *rain check*? 다음에 해도 될까요?
Thanks for telling me in *advance*. 미리 말해 줘서 고마워요.
plan · appointment · conference

친구와 놀 약속에는 *plan(s)*가 자연스럽고, *appointment*는 병원·업무 등 정해진 면담이나 예약에 자주 써요. 큰 회의·학회는 *conference*.
(참고) Problems can *occur*. 문제는 생길 수 있어요.(글에서 쓰는 말) 말할 땐 Something came up.
steps.blank:
A: Can we ___ our plan? How about Sunday ___?
B: Let me check my ___. Sunday at two? That ___ for me.
낱말 상자: change · instead · schedule · works
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 미루기·취소하기: postpone = put off 미루다 / cancel 취소하다 · The train is delayed. 기차가 늦어져요. / Can I take a rain check? 다음에 해도 될까요? / Thanks for telling me in advance. 미리 말해 줘서 고마워요.
- plan · appointment · conference: 친구와 놀 약속에는 plan(s)가 자연스럽고, appointment는 병원·업무 등 정해진 면담이나 예약에 자주 써요. 큰 회의·학회는 conference. / (참고) Problems can occur. 문제는 생길 수 있어요.(글에서 쓰는 말) 말할 땐 Something came up.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Can we ___ our plan? How about Sunday ___? / B: Let me check my ___. Sunday at two? That ___ for me. / 낱말 상자: change · instead · schedule · works
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: calendar (달력), schedule (일정), appointment ((병원 등) 예약), conference (큰 회의, 학회), cancel (취소하다), delay (늦어짐, 지연), postpone (미루다), change (바꾸다), earlier (더 일찍), later (나중에). Review words: sorry (미안한), fine (괜찮은).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: Can I take a rain check?
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: instead (대신에) — "How about Sunday instead?"; until (~까지) — "until next week"; available ((시간이) 되는) — "I’m available after one."; suddenly (갑자기) — "Suddenly, it started to snow."; rain check (다음 기회(로 미루기)) — "Can I take a rain check?"; work ((날·시간이) 괜찮다; 일하다) — "That works for me."; except (~만 빼고) — "every day except Monday"; advance (미리(in advance); 나아가다) — "Tell me in advance.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: A friend says, “Can we change our plan?” What do you say?
Something came up. Tell your friend.
I’m so sorry about this. Something came up.
I say, “How about Friday at seven?” But you are busy. What do you say?
That doesn’t work for me. How about ___?
When are you usually available to meet friends?
Do you use a calendar on your phone or on paper?
I use ___. / I don’t use a calendar.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "A friend says, “Can we change our plan?” What do you say?" (hint on screen: Sure. How about ___ instead?)
- "Something came up. Tell your friend." (hint on screen: I’m so sorry about this. Something came up.)
- "I say, “How about Friday at seven?” But you are busy. What do you say?" (hint on screen: That doesn’t work for me. How about ___?)
- "When are you usually available to meet friends?" (hint on screen: I’m usually available on ___.)
- "Do you use a calendar on your phone or on paper?" (hint on screen: I use ___. / I don’t use a calendar.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Sunday at the Rink
steps.text: Every winter, the town *puts up* an outdoor skating rink near the park. It is open every day except Monday. Jiwoo and Ben wanted to go on Saturday morning, but Jiwoo suddenly had to work. It had *to do with* a client’s website. Changes like this occur all the time, and Ben didn’t mind. On Sunday, they met at two. They skated for an hour *or so*. Then Ben *pulled out* his phone and took a picture of Jiwoo with her hot chocolate. Next time, she is going to tell Ben about changes in advance.
steps.gloss: put up 세우다, 설치하다 · to do with ~와 관련된 · or so ~쯤 · pull out 꺼내다 · occur 생기다, 일어나다 · in advance 미리
questions: Why did Jiwoo change the plan?
How long did they skate?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Sunday at the Rink". Text: "Every winter, the town puts up an outdoor skating rink near the park. It is open every day except Monday. Jiwoo and Ben wanted to go on Saturday morning, but Jiwoo suddenly had to work. It had to do with a client’s website. Changes like this occur all the time, and Ben didn’t mind. On Sunday, they met at two. They skated for an hour or so. Then Ben pulled out his phone and took a picture of Jiwoo with her hot chocolate. Next time, she is going to tell Ben about changes in advance." Words: put up 세우다, 설치하다 · to do with ~와 관련된 · or so ~쯤 · pull out 꺼내다 · occur 생기다, 일어나다 · in advance 미리.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why did Jiwoo change the plan?" / "How long did they skate?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Can we change our plan?’으로 약속을 바꾸자고 할 수 있어요.
‘How about ___ instead?’로 다른 날·시간을 제안할 수 있어요.
‘That works for me.’로 좋다고, ‘That doesn’t work for me.’로 안 된다고 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Can we change our plan?’으로 약속을 바꾸자고 할 수 있어요.
- ‘How about ___ instead?’로 다른 날·시간을 제안할 수 있어요.
- ‘That works for me.’로 좋다고, ‘That doesn’t work for me.’로 안 된다고 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 추천해 줄래요?
steps.title_en: Can you recommend a good book?
steps.goal: 추천을 부탁하고, 추천하고, 반응하기
steps.scene_desc: 2월 오후, 동네 모퉁이 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼이 책 한 권을 지우에게 건네고, 지우는 웃으며 공책에 메모함(책 표지·공책 글자는 보이지 않게)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Can you recommend a good book?" (추천해 줄래요?). Goal: 추천을 부탁하고, 추천하고, 반응하기. Today's scene: 2월 오후, 동네 모퉁이 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼이 책 한 권을 지우에게 건네고, 지우는 웃으며 공책에 메모함(책 표지·공책 글자는 보이지 않게). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Can you recommend a good ___?".

steps.when: 책·식당·TV 프로그램 같은 걸 추천해 달라고 할 때 써요.
steps.extra: Can you recommend a good book? · a good café?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Can you recommend a good ___?" (좋은 ~ 추천해 줄래요?). When to use it: 책·식당·TV 프로그램 같은 걸 추천해 달라고 할 때 써요. Note: Can you recommend a good book? · a good café?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "You should try ___.".

steps.when: 상대에게 권할 때 써요. try는 ‘읽어 보다·먹어 보다·해 보다’ 모두 돼요.
steps.extra: You should try this book. · You should try the soup.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "You should try ___." (~ 한번 해 봐요.). When to use it: 상대에게 권할 때 써요. try는 ‘읽어 보다·먹어 보다·해 보다’ 모두 돼요. Note: You should try this book. · You should try the soup.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "That sounds great!".

steps.when: 추천을 듣고 반갑게 대답할 때 써요.
steps.extra: That sounds fun! · That sounds interesting!
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "That sounds great!" (좋네요!). When to use it: 추천을 듣고 반갑게 대답할 때 써요. Note: That sounds fun! · That sounds interesting!
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Good Books · 2월 오후, 동네 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Good Books · 2월 오후, 동네 카페에서

lines.en: Daniel, {{can you recommend a good}} book for my English study?
lines.ko: 대니얼, 영어 공부에 좋은 책 추천해 줄래요?

lines.en: Sure. What kind of books do you like?
lines.ko: 그럼요. 어떤 책을 좋아해요?

lines.en: I like fiction, but long books are hard for me. What do you suggest?
lines.ko: 소설을 좋아하는데, 긴 책은 어려워요. 뭘 추천해요?

lines.en: {{You should try}} “Max and the Moon Café.” It’s a fiction series, and it’s really popular.
lines.ko: ‘맥스와 달빛 카페’를 읽어 봐요. 소설 시리즈인데 인기가 정말 많아요.

lines.en: Is it easy?
lines.ko: 쉬워요?

lines.en: Yes. Here’s why. Each chapter is only five pages, so you can read it on your own.
lines.ko: 네. 왜냐하면요, 한 장이 다섯 쪽뿐이라 혼자서도 읽을 수 있어요.

lines.en: Okay, I’ll check it out. What about TV shows?
lines.ko: 좋아요, 찾아볼게요. TV 프로그램은요?

lines.en: You should watch “Pine Hill Neighbors.” It’s funny. You won’t regret it.

head: 무엇을
이렇게 추천해요
rows: You should try this book. It’s really popular.
You should try the local noodle place.
You should go to the café near the station.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Can you recommend a good ___? / You should try ___. / You should ___. Table (무엇을 → 이렇게 추천해요):
- book 책 → You should try this book. It’s really popular.
- TV show TV 프로그램 → You should watch “Pine Hill Neighbors.”
- restaurant 식당 → You should try the local noodle place.
- café 카페 → You should go to the café near the station.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
‘~해 봐요, ~하는 게 좋아요’ 하고 권할 때: You *should try* this book.
하지 않는 게 좋을 때: You *shouldn’t* start with book ten.

물을 때는 should가 앞으로: *Should I* read it in English?
What *should I* watch?
주어가 he·she여도 should 뒤에는 동사원형: She should *try* it.
errors: You should to try this book.
should 뒤에는 to 없이 바로 동사.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- should + 동사원형: ‘~해 봐요, ~하는 게 좋아요’ 하고 권할 때: You should try this book. / 하지 않는 게 좋을 때: You shouldn’t start with book ten.
- Should I ~?: 물을 때는 should가 앞으로: Should I read it in English? / What should I watch? / 주어가 he·she여도 should 뒤에는 동사원형: She should try it.
Common mistakes on screen:
- You should to try this book. → You should try this book. (should 뒤에는 to 없이 바로 동사.)
- She should reads it. → She should read it. (주어가 she라도 should 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- Is it worth? → Is it worth it? (worth 뒤의 it을 빼지 않아요.)
- That’s sound great! → That sounds great! (sound가 동사예요. That sounds ~ (~하게 들려요))
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "Can you recommend a good book?" (추천해 줄래요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Can you recommend a good ___?" / "You should try ___." / "That sounds great!". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 추천 부탁하기·묻기: "What do you suggest?" (뭘 추천해요?, 보통); "Do you know any good places?" (좋은 곳 알아요?, 보통); "Is it worth it?" (그만한 가치가 있어요?, 보통)
- 추천하기: "It’s really popular." (정말 인기 많아요., 보통); "I’ve heard good things about it." (좋다는 얘기 들었어요., 보통); "You won’t regret it." (후회 안 할 거예요., 친근); "Totally worth it." (완전 그만한 가치가 있어요., 친근)

Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.

Picture words on screen. New: book (책), television (텔레비전), series (시리즈), author (작가), fiction (소설, 지어낸 이야기), edition ((책의) 판), review (후기, 리뷰), famous (유명한), popular (인기 있는), local (동네의, 그 지역의), tip (조언, 도움말), menu (메뉴).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.

items: Can you recommend a good book?
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: recommend (추천하다) — "Can you recommend a good book?"; recommendation (추천) — "Thanks for the recommendation."; suggest (권하다, 제안하다) — "What do you suggest?"; try (해 보다, 먹어 보다) — "You should try it."; worth (~할 가치가 있는) — "Totally worth it."; regret (후회하다) — "You won’t regret it."; highly (아주, 매우) — "I highly recommend it."; check (확인하다, 알아보다) — "I’ll check it out."; show ((TV) 프로그램, 쇼) — "a funny TV show"; place (곳, 장소) — "a good place for lunch".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Can you recommend a good book or TV show?" (hint on screen: You should try ___. It’s really popular.)
- "What kind of books do you like?" (hint on screen: I like ___. / I don’t read much.)
- "I want to try Korean food. What do you suggest?" (hint on screen: You should try ___. You won’t regret it.)
- "Is there a show you really love? Is it worth it?" (hint on screen: Yes, totally worth it. / It’s okay.)
- "Ask me for a recommendation." (hint on screen: Can you recommend a good ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s Reading Plan
steps.text: After coffee, Jiwoo visits a local bookstore and finds “Max and the Moon Café.” The author is not very famous, but the series is popular, and the reviews are great. The new edition is cheap because the price *went down* last month. Daniel’s tip was helpful because the book is easy and fun. Jiwoo wasn’t aware of the word list at the back, but now she can refer to it for new words. She reads ten pages *on her own* every day.

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why is the new edition cheap?" / "How many pages does Jiwoo read every day?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.

steps.scene_desc: 2월 저녁, 동네 카페 테이블. 지우가 휴대폰으로 노트북 두 대 사진(작은 것과 큰 것)을 대니얼에게 보여 주고, 대니얼이 손가락 두 개를 들어 비교하며 이야기함(화면에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Which is better?" (뭐가 더 좋아요?). Goal: 둘을 비교하고 내 생각과 이유 말하기. Today's scene: 2월 저녁, 동네 카페 테이블. 지우가 휴대폰으로 노트북 두 대 사진(작은 것과 큰 것)을 대니얼에게 보여 주고, 대니얼이 손가락 두 개를 들어 비교하며 이야기함(화면에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Which is better, ___ or ___?".

steps.when: 둘 중 하나를 고를 때 상대 생각을 물어요.
steps.extra: Which is better, tea or coffee?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Which is better, ___ or ___?" (~랑 ~ 중에 뭐가 더 나아요?). When to use it: 둘 중 하나를 고를 때 상대 생각을 물어요. Note: Which is better, tea or coffee?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I think ___ is better.".

steps.when: 내 생각을 부드럽게 말해요.
steps.extra: I think the small one is better.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I think ___ is better." (~가 더 나은 것 같아요.). When to use it: 내 생각을 부드럽게 말해요. Note: I think the small one is better.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "It’s ___er than ___.".

steps.when: 이유를 비교해서 말해요. 긴 말은 more ~.
steps.extra: It’s lighter than the big one. · It’s more comfortable.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "It’s ___er than ___." (~보다 더 ~해요.). When to use it: 이유를 비교해서 말해요. 긴 말은 more ~. Note: It’s lighter than the big one. · It’s more comfortable.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Two Laptops · 2월 저녁, 동네 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Two Laptops · 2월 저녁, 동네 카페에서

lines.en: Daniel, I need a new laptop for work. {{Which is better,}} this one {{or}} that one?
lines.ko: 대니얼, 일할 때 쓸 노트북이 필요해요. 이거랑 저거 중에 뭐가 더 나아요?

lines.en: Hmm. Compare these two. This model has a 13-inch screen. That one has a 16-inch screen.
lines.ko: 음. 이 둘을 비교해 봐요. 이 모델은 13인치 화면이고, 저건 16인치예요.

lines.en: Right. The big one has a wider screen, but the small one is much cheaper.
lines.ko: 맞아요. 큰 건 화면이 더 넓은데, 작은 게 훨씬 싸요.

lines.en: What about the other features?
lines.ko: 다른 기능은요?

lines.en: They’re about the same. Both are good.
lines.ko: 거의 같아요. 둘 다 좋아요.

lines.en: Then it depends. Do you carry it a lot?
lines.ko: 그럼 경우에 따라 달라요. 많이 들고 다녀요?

lines.en: Yes. To the office, to cafés, everywhere!
lines.ko: 네. 사무실에도, 카페에도, 어디든요!

lines.en: Then {{I think}} the small one {{is better}}. {{It’s}} light{{er than}} the big one.
lines.ko: 그럼 작은 게 더 나은 것 같아요. 큰 것보다 가벼워요.

lines.en: But I’m a designer. A big screen is easier for my work.
lines.ko: 하지만 전 디자이너예요. 큰 화면이 일하기 더 편해요.

lines.en: True. Neither is perfect. Is there a big monitor at your office?
lines.ko: 맞아요. 둘 다 완벽하진 않네요. 사무실에 큰 모니터 있어요?

lines.en: Yes, there is! Okay, I prefer the small one.
lines.ko: 네, 있어요! 좋아요, 작은 게 더 좋겠어요.

If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.

frame: I think ___ is better. It’s ___er than ___.
head: 원래 말
비교급
이렇게 말해요
rows: The small one is lighter than the big one.
The small one is much cheaper.
This phone is easier to use.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Which is better, ___ or ___? / I think ___ is better. It’s ___er than ___. Table (원래 말 → 비교급):
- light 가벼운 → lighter
- cheap 싼 → cheaper
- easy 쉬운 → easier
- comfortable 편한 → more comfortable
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
짧은 말 + *-er*: light → lighter · fast → faster
-y로 끝나면: easy → easier
긴 말은 앞에 *more*: more comfortable · more convenient
따로 외워요: good → *better* · bad → *worse*

비교하는 대상 앞에 *than*: It’s lighter *than* the big one.
‘훨씬’은 *much*: It’s *much* cheaper.
‘~만큼 좋진 않아요’: It’s not as good as the big one.
errors: It’s lighter then the big one.
It’s lighter than the big one.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 비교급 만들기: 짧은 말 + -er: light → lighter · fast → faster / -y로 끝나면: easy → easier / 긴 말은 앞에 more: more comfortable · more convenient / 따로 외워요: good → better · bad → worse
- than · much: 비교하는 대상 앞에 than: It’s lighter than the big one. / ‘훨씬’은 much: It’s much cheaper. / ‘~만큼 좋진 않아요’: It’s not as good as the big one.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s more cheaper. → It’s cheaper. (-er과 more를 함께 쓰지 않아요.)
- It’s lighter then the big one. → It’s lighter than the big one. (‘~보다’는 than. (then은 ‘그때, 그러면’))
- This one is gooder. → This one is better. (good의 비교급은 better.)
- It’s very cheaper. → It’s much cheaper. (비교급 앞 ‘훨씬’은 much. (very ×))
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: 비교급 만들기: 짧은 말 + -er: light → lighter · fast → faster-y로 끝나면: easy → easier긴 말은 앞에 more: more comfortable · more convenient따로 외워요: good → better · bad → worse
than · much: 비교하는 대상 앞에 than: It’s lighter than the big one.‘훨씬’은 much: It’s much cheaper.‘~만큼 좋진 않아요’: It’s not as good as the big one.

It’s lighter then the big one. → It’s lighter than the big one.
This one is gooder. → This one is better.
It’s very cheaper. → It’s much cheaper.

steps.note: 예) fast / the bus · the subway → Which is faster, the bus or the subway? — I think the subway is faster.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) fast / the bus · the subway → Which is faster, the bus or the subway? — I think the subway is faster. Items (situation → model answer): fast → the bus · the subway | cheap → this laptop · that laptop | easy → this phone · that phone | comfortable → the sofa · the chair.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "Which is better?" (뭐가 더 좋아요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Which is better, ___ or ___?" / "I think ___ is better." / "It’s ___er than ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 비교해서 말하기: "It’s more comfortable." (더 편해요., 보통); "It’s much cheaper." (훨씬 싸요., 보통); "It’s easier to use." (쓰기가 더 쉬워요., 보통); "It’s not as good as ___." (~만큼 좋지는 않아요., 보통)
- 비슷할 때·정하기 어려울 때: "They’re about the same." (거의 같아요., 보통); "It depends." (경우에 따라 달라요., 보통); "Both are good." (둘 다 좋아요., 친근)
- 고르기: "I prefer ___." (저는 ~가 더 좋아요., 보통); "Neither is perfect." (둘 다 완벽하진 않아요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

A: Which do you ___, tea or coffee?   B: ___ are good!
낱말 상자: better · er · than · prefer · Both
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- prefer · depend: I prefer the small one. 작은 게 더 좋아요. / It depends on your preference. 취향에 따라 달라요. / both 둘 다 · neither 둘 다 아닌
- 크기·값 말하기: a 13-inch screen 13인치 화면(1인치 ≈ 2.5cm) / one meter wide 폭 1미터 / the average price 평균 가격 · a price range 가격대
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: Which is ___, the bus or the subway? B: I think the subway is better. It’s fast___ ___ the bus. / A: Which do you ___, tea or coffee? B: ___ are good! / 낱말 상자: better · er · than · prefer · Both
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: more (더 많은), less (더 적은), faster (더 빠른), easier (더 쉬운), comfortable (편한), convenient (편리한), both (둘 다), neither (둘 다 아닌), different (다른), similar (비슷한), average (평균(의)), range (범위, ~대).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: than (~보다) — "lighter than the big one"; better (더 좋은(good의 비교급)) — "Which is better?"; worse (더 나쁜(bad의 비교급)) — "The traffic is worse today."; cheaper (더 싼) — "It’s much cheaper."; same (같은) — "They’re about the same."; prefer (더 좋아하다) — "I prefer tea."; depend (~에 달려 있다) — "It depends."; basic (기본적인) — "basic features"; model ((제품의) 모델) — "this laptop model"; feature (기능, 특징) — "the same features".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Which is better, coffee or tea?" (hint on screen: I think ___ is better. / I prefer ___.)
- "Which is better for you, a laptop or a tablet? Why?" (hint on screen: I think ___ is better. It’s ___er / more ___.)
- "Which do you prefer, summer or winter?" (hint on screen: I prefer ___. It’s ___er than ___.)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s New Laptop
steps.text: On Saturday, Jiwoo buys the small model. Despite its smaller screen, she loves it. It’s much lighter, so she can take it *all over* the city. Her desk at work is only one *meter* *wide*, so the small one is better *after all*. The box contains a charger and a soft cover. She puts the empty box on the shelf above her desk. On Monday, Chloe sees the laptop. “Ooh, it’s so light! Perfect for travel!” In April, Chloe is going to visit her family home in Toronto. “Come with me, Jiwoo! You can stay at my parents’ house.” “Really?” “Of course! *Go ahead* and look for a ticket!”
steps.gloss: despite ~에도 불구하고 · all over 곳곳에 · after all 결국 · contain 들어 있다 · above ~ 위에 · family home 고향 집 · go ahead 어서 ~해요
questions: Why is the small laptop better for Jiwoo’s desk?
Where is Chloe going in April?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Jiwoo’s New Laptop". Text: "On Saturday, Jiwoo buys the small model. Despite its smaller screen, she loves it. It’s much lighter, so she can take it all over the city. Her desk at work is only one meter wide, so the small one is better after all. The box contains a charger and a soft cover. She puts the empty box on the shelf above her desk. On Monday, Chloe sees the laptop. “Ooh, it’s so light! Perfect for travel!” In April, Chloe is going to visit her family home in Toronto. “Come with me, Jiwoo! You can stay at my parents’ house.” “Really?” “Of course! Go ahead and look for a ticket!”" Words: despite ~에도 불구하고 · all over 곳곳에 · after all 결국 · contain 들어 있다 · above ~ 위에 · family home 고향 집 · go ahead 어서 ~해요.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why is the small laptop better for Jiwoo’s desk?" / "Where is Chloe going in April?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘Which is better, ___ or ___?’로 둘 중 뭐가 나은지 물을 수 있어요.
‘I think ___ is better.’로 내 생각을 말할 수 있어요.
‘It’s ___er than ___.’로 둘을 비교해 이유를 말할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘Which is better, ___ or ___?’로 둘 중 뭐가 나은지 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I think ___ is better.’로 내 생각을 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s ___er than ___.’로 둘을 비교해 이유를 말할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 최고는 어디예요?
steps.title_en: What’s the best bakery in town?
steps.goal: 가장 좋은 것을 묻고 최상급으로 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 2월 말 토요일 아침, 아파트 앞 동네 길. 갓 산 빵 봉투를 든 벤이 길 저쪽을 손으로 가리키고, 지우가 고개를 끄덕이며 들음(간판 글자는 보이지 않게)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What’s the best bakery in town?" (최고는 어디예요?). Goal: 가장 좋은 것을 묻고 최상급으로 말하기. Today's scene: 2월 말 토요일 아침, 아파트 앞 동네 길. 갓 산 빵 봉투를 든 벤이 길 저쪽을 손으로 가리키고, 지우가 고개를 끄덕이며 들음(간판 글자는 보이지 않게). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What’s the best ___ in town?".

steps.when: 동네에서 가장 좋은 가게·식당을 물을 때 써요. in town은 ‘이 동네(도시)에서’.
steps.extra: What’s the best bakery in town? · the best noodle place
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What’s the best ___ in town?" (이 동네에서 제일 좋은 ~는 어디예요?). When to use it: 동네에서 가장 좋은 가게·식당을 물을 때 써요. in town은 ‘이 동네(도시)에서’. Note: What’s the best bakery in town? · the best noodle place.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "It’s the ___est ___ I know.".

steps.when: 최상급으로 ‘가장 ~한’을 말해요. 긴 말은 *the most* ~.
steps.extra: It’s the oldest bakery I know. · the most popular café
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "It’s the ___est ___ I know." (제가 아는 ~ 중에 제일 ~해요.). When to use it: 최상급으로 ‘가장 ~한’을 말해요. 긴 말은 the most ~. Note: It’s the oldest bakery I know. · the most popular café.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "You can’t miss it.".

steps.when: 길을 알려 준 뒤 ‘찾기 쉬워요, 놓칠 리 없어요’ 하고 덧붙여요.
steps.extra: It’s next to the flower shop. You can’t miss it.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "You can’t miss it." (바로 보일 거예요.). When to use it: 길을 알려 준 뒤 ‘찾기 쉬워요, 놓칠 리 없어요’ 하고 덧붙여요. Note: It’s next to the flower shop. You can’t miss it.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("The Best Bakery · 2월 말 토요일 아침, 동네 길에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: The Best Bakery · 2월 말 토요일 아침, 동네 길에서

lines.en: Morning, Ben! What’s in the bag?
lines.ko: 좋은 아침이에요, 벤! 봉투에 뭐 있어요?

lines.en: Fresh bread! I wake up early every Saturday for this.
lines.ko: 갓 구운 빵이요! 이거 때문에 토요일마다 일찍 일어나요.

lines.en: Chloe and Maya are coming for brunch tomorrow. Where is the most delicious bakery here?
lines.ko: 내일 클로이랑 마야가 브런치 먹으러 와요. 여기서 제일 맛있는 빵집이 어디예요?

lines.en: Not bad! But here’s how people really say it: “{{What’s the best}} bakery {{in town}}?”
lines.ko: 나쁘지 않아요! 근데 사람들은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “What’s the best bakery in town?”

lines.en: Ha! What’s the best bakery in town?
lines.ko: 하하! 이 동네 최고의 빵집은 어디예요?

lines.en: This one, by far. {{It’s the}} old{{est}} bakery {{I know}}. It’s on the way to the station. {{You can’t miss it}}.
lines.ko: 단연 여기예요. 제가 아는 제일 오래된 빵집이에요. 역 가는 길에 있어요. 바로 보일 거예요.

lines.en: Is it crowded?
lines.ko: 사람 많아요?

lines.en: Always. The line is long, but it’s worth the wait.
lines.ko: 늘요. 줄이 길지만 기다릴 만해요.

lines.en: And what’s the best noodle place?
lines.ko: 그리고 제일 좋은 국숫집은요?

lines.en: In my opinion, the little place across from the park. It’s the cheapest, and the soup is fantastic.
lines.ko: 제 생각엔 공원 건너편 작은 집이요. 제일 싸고, 국물이 끝내줘요.

lines.en: Thanks, Ben! I’ll try both.
lines.ko: 고마워요, 벤! 둘 다 가 볼게요.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The Best Bakery · 2월 말 토요일 아침, 동네 길에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Jiwoo: "Morning, Ben! What’s in the bag?" (좋은 아침이에요, 벤! 봉투에 뭐 있어요?)
2. Ben: "Fresh bread! I wake up early every Saturday for this." (갓 구운 빵이요! 이거 때문에 토요일마다 일찍 일어나요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Chloe and Maya are coming for brunch tomorrow. Where is the most delicious bakery here?" (내일 클로이랑 마야가 브런치 먹으러 와요. 여기서 제일 맛있는 빵집이 어디예요?)
4. Ben: "Not bad! But here’s how people really say it: “What’s the best bakery in town?”" (나쁘지 않아요! 근데 사람들은 실제로 이렇게 말해요. “What’s the best bakery in town?”)
5. Jiwoo: "Ha! What’s the best bakery in town?" (하하! 이 동네 최고의 빵집은 어디예요?)
6. Ben: "This one, by far. It’s the oldest bakery I know. It’s on the way to the station. You can’t miss it." (단연 여기예요. 제가 아는 제일 오래된 빵집이에요. 역 가는 길에 있어요. 바로 보일 거예요.)
7. Jiwoo: "Is it crowded?" (사람 많아요?)
8. Ben: "Always. The line is long, but it’s worth the wait." (늘요. 줄이 길지만 기다릴 만해요.)
9. Jiwoo: "And what’s the best noodle place?" (그리고 제일 좋은 국숫집은요?)
10. Ben: "In my opinion, the little place across from the park. It’s the cheapest, and the soup is fantastic." (제 생각엔 공원 건너편 작은 집이요. 제일 싸고, 국물이 끝내줘요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Thanks, Ben! I’ll try both." (고마워요, 벤! 둘 다 가 볼게요.)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

8. Ben: "Always. The line is long, but it’s worth the wait." (늘요. 줄이 길지만 기다릴 만해요.)
9. Jiwoo: "And what’s the best noodle place?" (그리고 제일 좋은 국숫집은요?)
10. Ben: "In my opinion, the little place across from the park. It’s the cheapest, and the soup is fantastic." (제 생각엔 공원 건너편 작은 집이요. 제일 싸고, 국물이 끝내줘요.)
11. Jiwoo: "Thanks, Ben! I’ll try both." (고마워요, 벤! 둘 다 가 볼게요.)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

frame: It’s the ___est ___ I know. You can’t miss it.
head: 원래 말
최상급
이렇게 말해요
rows: It’s the oldest bakery I know.
It’s the biggest park in town.
It’s the most popular café around here.
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What’s the best ___ in town? / It’s the ___est ___ I know. You can’t miss it. Table (원래 말 → 최상급):
- old 오래된 → the oldest
- cheap 싼 → the cheapest
- big 큰 → the biggest
- popular 인기 있는 → the most popular
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
짧은 말 + *-est*: old → oldest · near → nearest
끝 글자를 하나 더: big → biggest
긴 말은 앞에 *the most*: the most popular
따로 외워요: good → *best* · bad → *worst*

최상급 앞에는 보통 *the*: It’s *the* best bakery.
‘~ 중에서’는 뒤에: in town · around here · I know
‘가장 덜 ~한’은 the least: the least crowded time
errors: It’s the best bakery in town.
It’s one of the best bakery.
It’s one of the best bakeries.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 최상급 만들기: 짧은 말 + -est: old → oldest · near → nearest / 끝 글자를 하나 더: big → biggest / 긴 말은 앞에 the most: the most popular / 따로 외워요: good → best · bad → worst
- the + 최상급 + 범위: 최상급 앞에는 보통 the: It’s the best bakery. / ‘~ 중에서’는 뒤에: in town · around here · I know / ‘가장 덜 ~한’은 the least: the least crowded time
Common mistakes on screen:
- It’s the most oldest bakery. → It’s the oldest bakery. (-est와 most를 함께 쓰지 않아요.)
- It’s best bakery in town. → It’s the best bakery in town. (최상급 앞에는 the.)
- This café is the goodest. → This café is the best. (good의 최상급은 best.)
- It’s one of the best bakery. → It’s one of the best bakeries. (one of the 뒤에는 복수.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) bakery / old → What’s the best bakery in town? — This one. It’s the oldest bakery I know.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) bakery / old → What’s the best bakery in town? — This one. It’s the oldest bakery I know. Items (situation → model answer): bakery → old | noodle place → cheap | park → big | café → popular.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "What’s the best bakery in town?" (최고는 어디예요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What’s the best ___ in town?" / "It’s the ___est ___ I know." / "You can’t miss it.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: It’s the most popular place around here.
이 근처에서 제일 인기 있는 곳이에요.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 최고를 말하기: "It’s the most popular place around here." (이 근처에서 제일 인기 있는 곳이에요., 보통); "It’s one of the best." (최고 중 하나예요., 보통); "By far the best." (단연 최고예요., 친근); "It’s the cheapest one." (제일 싼 곳이에요., 보통)
- 내 생각·평 말하기: "In my opinion, ___." (제 생각에는 ~., 정중); "Everyone loves it." (다들 좋아해요., 보통); "That’s the worst." (그건 최악이에요., 친근)
- 붐빌 때: "It’s always crowded." (늘 붐벼요., 보통); "It’s worth the wait." (기다릴 만해요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: the least · one of the best

Early morning is *the least* crowded time. 아침 일찍이 사람이 제일 적어요.
It’s *one of the best* bakeries. 최고 중 하나예요.(뒤에 복수)
Rainy Mondays are *the worst*. 비 오는 월요일이 최악이에요.
순위·곳 말하기

the *top* ten 상위 10 · *rank* first 1위를 하다
the best *spot* for a *view* 경치 보기 제일 좋은 곳
in the *capital* · in this *region* · in the *nation* 수도에서 · 이 지역에서 · 전국에서
steps.blank:
A: What’s the ___ bakery in town?   B: This one. It’s the old___ bakery I know.
A: Is it far?   B: No. It’s on the way to the station. You can’t ___ it.
낱말 상자: best · est · miss
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- the least · one of the best: Early morning is the least crowded time. 아침 일찍이 사람이 제일 적어요. / It’s one of the best bakeries. 최고 중 하나예요.(뒤에 복수) / Rainy Mondays are the worst. 비 오는 월요일이 최악이에요.
- 순위·곳 말하기: the top ten 상위 10 · rank first 1위를 하다 / the best spot for a view 경치 보기 제일 좋은 곳 / in the capital · in this region · in the nation 수도에서 · 이 지역에서 · 전국에서
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What’s the ___ bakery in town? B: This one. It’s the old___ bakery I know. / A: Is it far? B: No. It’s on the way to the station. You can’t ___ it. / 낱말 상자: best · est · miss
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: town (동네, 소도시), crowded (붐비는), line (줄), view (경치, 전망), spot (곳, 자리), top (맨 위, 1위), rank (순위(를 매기다)), capital (수도), central (중심의, 중앙의), region (지역), nation (나라, 국가), giant (거대한).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: It’s the best bakery in town.
In my opinion, it’s the best.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: most (가장(긴 말 앞)) — "the most popular place"; least (가장 덜) — "the least crowded time"; best (가장 좋은(good의 최상급)) — "It’s the best bakery in town."; worst (가장 나쁜(bad의 최상급)) — "That’s the worst."; everyone (모든 사람, 다들) — "Everyone loves it."; opinion (의견) — "In my opinion, it’s the best."; wait (기다리다; 기다림) — "It’s worth the wait."; lovely (아주 좋은, 아름다운) — "What a lovely view!"; brilliant (훌륭한, 아주 멋진) — "The soup was brilliant!"; impressive (인상적인, 대단한) — "The view is impressive.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What’s the best café you know? Why?
It’s ___. It’s the ___est café I know.
In your opinion, what’s the most popular food in Korea?
In my opinion, ___ is the most popular.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What’s the best café you know? Why?" (hint on screen: It’s ___. It’s the ___est café I know.)
- "In your opinion, what’s the most popular food in Korea?" (hint on screen: In my opinion, ___ is the most popular.)
- "What’s the best season for a trip in Korea?" (hint on screen: I think ___ is the best. The views are lovely.)
- "Is there a place that’s always crowded but worth the wait?" (hint on screen: Yes, ___. It’s always crowded, but it’s worth the wait.)
- "What’s the worst thing about crowded places?" (hint on screen: The worst thing is ___.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
