steps.title: The Oldest Bakery in Town
steps.text: On Sunday, Jiwoo *wakes up* at six thirty. The bakery is *on the way* to the station, and Ben was right: you can’t miss it. There is a giant bread sign over the door. Two sisters established the bakery in 1985 in a former bank building. Now it sells *a variety of* breads and cakes. Jiwoo waits in line for twenty minutes and buys the most popular bread. At brunch, Chloe takes a bite. “Fantastic! It’s the best bread in Seoul!” Maya nods. “It’s impressive. A food website ranked it in the top ten in the nation last year.” Jiwoo smiles. It was worth the wait.
steps.gloss: wake up 잠에서 깨다 · on the way ~ 가는 길에 · a variety of 여러 가지의 · sign 간판 · establish 세우다, 차리다 · former 예전의, 전에 ~였던 · rank 순위를 매기다
questions: Who established the bakery?
What did a food website do last year?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "The Oldest Bakery in Town". Text: "On Sunday, Jiwoo wakes up at six thirty. The bakery is on the way to the station, and Ben was right: you can’t miss it. There is a giant bread sign over the door. Two sisters established the bakery in 1985 in a former bank building. Now it sells a variety of breads and cakes. Jiwoo waits in line for twenty minutes and buys the most popular bread. At brunch, Chloe takes a bite. “Fantastic! It’s the best bread in Seoul!” Maya nods. “It’s impressive. A food website ranked it in the top ten in the nation last year.” Jiwoo smiles. It was worth the wait." Words: wake up 잠에서 깨다 · on the way ~ 가는 길에 · a variety of 여러 가지의 · sign 간판 · establish 세우다, 차리다 · former 예전의, 전에 ~였던 · rank 순위를 매기다.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Who established the bakery?" / "What did a food website do last year?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What’s the best ___ in town?’으로 동네 최고의 곳을 물을 수 있어요.
‘It’s the ___est ___ I know.’로 최상급을 써서 말할 수 있어요.
‘You can’t miss it.’으로 찾기 쉽다고 덧붙일 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What’s the best ___ in town?’으로 동네 최고의 곳을 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘It’s the ___est ___ I know.’로 최상급을 써서 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘You can’t miss it.’으로 찾기 쉽다고 덧붙일 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 내일 비 오면
steps.goal: 조건에 따라 할 일을 말하고 대비하기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 금요일 오후, 동네 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼이 휴대폰 날씨 화면(구름·빗방울 그림만)을 지우에게 보여 주고, 지우는 접은 우산을 들어 보이며 웃음(글자는 보이지 않게)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "If it rains tomorrow…" (내일 비 오면). Goal: 조건에 따라 할 일을 말하고 대비하기. Today's scene: 3월 금요일 오후, 동네 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼이 휴대폰 날씨 화면(구름·빗방울 그림만)을 지우에게 보여 주고, 지우는 접은 우산을 들어 보이며 웃음(글자는 보이지 않게). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "If it rains tomorrow, ___.".

steps.when: 날씨에 따라 할 일을 말해요. if 쪽은 내일 일이어도 현재형(rains), 뒤쪽은 *will*.
steps.extra: If it rains tomorrow, we’ll go to the museum.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "If it rains tomorrow, ___." (내일 비가 오면 ~.). When to use it: 날씨에 따라 할 일을 말해요. if 쪽은 내일 일이어도 현재형(rains), 뒤쪽은 will. Note: If it rains tomorrow, we’ll go to the museum.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Let’s wait and see.".

steps.when: 지금 정하기 어려울 때 ‘좀 기다려 보자’고 해요.
steps.extra: Rain or no rain? Let’s wait and see.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Let’s wait and see." (두고 봐요.). When to use it: 지금 정하기 어려울 때 ‘좀 기다려 보자’고 해요. Note: Rain or no rain? Let’s wait and see.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "Just in case, ___.".

steps.when: 만일을 대비해 무언가를 하자고 할 때 써요.
steps.extra: Just in case, bring an umbrella.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "Just in case, ___." (혹시 모르니 ~.). When to use it: 만일을 대비해 무언가를 하자고 할 때 써요. Note: Just in case, bring an umbrella.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Plan B · 3월 금요일 오후, 동네 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: Plan B · 3월 금요일 오후, 동네 카페에서

lines.en: Daniel, are we still going to the hill park tomorrow?
lines.ko: 대니얼, 내일 뒷산 공원 가는 거 그대로죠?

lines.en: I hope so. But the forecast says there’s a sixty percent chance of rain.
lines.ko: 그러길 바라요. 근데 일기 예보에 비 올 확률이 60퍼센트래요.

lines.en: Oh no. What if it rains?
lines.ko: 이런. 비 오면요?

lines.en: {{If it rains tomorrow}}, we’ll go to the city museum instead. That’s Plan B.
lines.ko: 내일 비 오면 대신 시립 박물관에 가요. 그게 플랜 B예요.

lines.en: Good idea. But what if it’s closed?
lines.ko: 좋아요. 근데 문을 닫았으면요?

lines.en: It’s open every day. I checked.
lines.ko: 매일 열어요. 확인했어요.

lines.en: So, rain or no rain?
lines.ko: 그래서 비가 올까요, 안 올까요?

lines.en: {{Let’s wait and see}}. I’ll let you know in the morning.
lines.ko: 두고 봐요. 아침에 알려 줄게요.

lines.en: Should I bring an umbrella?
lines.ko: 우산 가져갈까요?

lines.en: Yes. And {{just in case}}, bring a jacket, too. Here’s why. It’s probably going to be windy up there.
lines.ko: 네. 그리고 혹시 모르니 재킷도 가져와요. 왜냐하면요, 위쪽은 아마 바람이 셀 거예요.

lines.en: Okay. I hope it doesn’t rain. Fingers crossed!
lines.ko: 알았어요. 비가 안 오면 좋겠어요. 행운을 빌어요!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "Plan B · 3월 금요일 오후, 동네 카페에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Jiwoo: "Daniel, are we still going to the hill park tomorrow?" (대니얼, 내일 뒷산 공원 가는 거 그대로죠?)
2. Daniel: "I hope so. But the forecast says there’s a sixty percent chance of rain." (그러길 바라요. 근데 일기 예보에 비 올 확률이 60퍼센트래요.)
3. Jiwoo: "Oh no. What if it rains?" (이런. 비 오면요?)
4. Daniel: "If it rains tomorrow, we’ll go to the city museum instead. That’s Plan B." (내일 비 오면 대신 시립 박물관에 가요. 그게 플랜 B예요.)
5. Jiwoo: "Good idea. But what if it’s closed?" (좋아요. 근데 문을 닫았으면요?)
6. Daniel: "It’s open every day. I checked." (매일 열어요. 확인했어요.)
7. Jiwoo: "So, rain or no rain?" (그래서 비가 올까요, 안 올까요?)
8. Daniel: "Let’s wait and see. I’ll let you know in the morning." (두고 봐요. 아침에 알려 줄게요.)
9. Jiwoo: "Should I bring an umbrella?" (우산 가져갈까요?)
10. Daniel: "Yes. And just in case, bring a jacket, too. Here’s why. It’s probably going to be windy up there." (네. 그리고 혹시 모르니 재킷도 가져와요. 왜냐하면요, 위쪽은 아마 바람이 셀 거예요.)

frame: Let’s wait and see. / Just in case, bring ___.
head: 조건 (If …)
할 일 (… will)

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: If it rains tomorrow, we’ll ___. / Let’s wait and see. / Just in case, bring ___. Table (조건 (If …) → 할 일 (… will)):
- If it rains tomorrow, → we’ll go to the museum instead.
- If it’s sunny, → we’ll go up the hill.
- If I finish early, → I’ll call you.
- If you’re free, → let’s meet up.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
‘~하면 ~할 거예요’: If it *rains* tomorrow, we*’ll* go to the museum.
내일 일이어도 if 쪽은 현재형! (will rain ×)
순서를 바꿔도 돼요: We’ll go if it’s sunny.

혹시 모르니: *Just in case*, bring an umbrella.
= Bring an umbrella *just in case*.
~하면 어떡해요?: *What if* it’s closed?
그렇다면: If that’s the case, …
errors: If it will rain tomorrow, we’ll stay home.
If it rains tomorrow, we’ll stay home.
주어 it이 빠졌어요. it’s = it is.
Bring a jacket in case of.
Bring a jacket just in case.
문장 끝에는 just in case. (in case of 뒤엔 명사)
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- if + 현재형, will: ‘~하면 ~할 거예요’: If it rains tomorrow, we’ll go to the museum. / 내일 일이어도 if 쪽은 현재형! (will rain ×) / 순서를 바꿔도 돼요: We’ll go if it’s sunny.
- just in case · What if ~?: 혹시 모르니: Just in case, bring an umbrella. / = Bring an umbrella just in case. / ~하면 어떡해요?: What if it’s closed? / 그렇다면: If that’s the case, …
Common mistakes on screen:
- If it will rain tomorrow, we’ll stay home. → If it rains tomorrow, we’ll stay home. (if 쪽은 내일 일이어도 현재형.)
- What if is closed? → What if it’s closed? (주어 it이 빠졌어요. it’s = it is.)
- I hope it doesn’t rains. → I hope it doesn’t rain. (doesn’t 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- Bring a jacket in case of. → Bring a jacket just in case. (문장 끝에는 just in case. (in case of 뒤엔 명사))
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) rains / go to the museum → If it rains tomorrow, we’ll go to the museum. Items (situation → model answer): rains → go to the museum | is sunny → go up the hill | is cold → stay at the café | snows → cancel the plan.

What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "If it rains tomorrow…" (내일 비 오면); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "If it rains tomorrow, ___." / "Let’s wait and see." / "Just in case, ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: If you’re free, let’s meet up.
If I finish early, I’ll call you.
Bring a jacket just in case.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 조건 말하기: "If you’re free, let’s meet up." (시간 되면 만나요., 친근); "If I finish early, I’ll call you." (일찍 끝나면 전화할게요., 보통); "What if it’s closed?" (문을 닫았으면 어떡해요?, 보통); "Plan B is ___." (플랜 B는 ~예요., 친근)
- 대비하기·정하기: "Bring a jacket just in case." (혹시 모르니 재킷 가져와요., 보통); "We’ll go anyway." (그래도 갈 거예요., 보통); "I’ll let you know." (알려 줄게요., 보통)
- 바라기: "I hope it doesn’t rain." (비가 안 오면 좋겠어요., 보통); "Fingers crossed!" (행운을 빌어요!, 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 날씨 예보 말

a 60% *chance* of rain 비 올 확률 60%

Plan B = a *backup* plan 대안

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 날씨 예보 말: The forecast says rain. 예보에 비 온대요. / a 60% chance of rain 비 올 확률 60% / It’s below zero. 영하예요. / strong wind · a storm · a flood 센 바람 · 폭풍 · 홍수
- anyway · backup: It’s cloudy, but we’ll go anyway. 그래도 갈 거예요. / Plan B = a backup plan 대안 / outdoor ↔ indoor 야외의 ↔ 실내의: 비 오면 indoor 계획으로!
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: ___ it rains tomorrow, we’ll go to the museum. B: What ___ it’s closed? / A: It’s open every day. Bring an umbrella just in ___. B: Okay. Fingers ___! / 낱말 상자: If · if · case · crossed
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: forecast (일기 예보), rain (비; 비가 오다), storm (폭풍), wind (바람), flood (홍수), ground (땅, 바닥), below (~ 아래(에)), outdoor (야외의), indoor (실내의), closed (닫힌, 문을 닫은). Review words: open (열려 있는, 문을 연), cancel (취소하다).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: If it rains, we’ll stay home.
Bring an umbrella just in case.
a sixty percent chance of rain
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: if (만약 ~하면) — "If it rains, we’ll stay home."; case (경우) — "Bring an umbrella just in case."; anyway (어쨌든, 그래도) — "We’ll go anyway."; backup (대안, 예비) — "a backup plan"; probably (아마) — "It’s probably going to rain."; chance (가능성, 확률) — "a sixty percent chance of rain"; hope (바라다) — "I hope it doesn’t rain."; plan (계획) — "Plan B is the museum.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What will you do this weekend if it rains?
What will you do if you finish work early today?
Do you check the weather forecast? When?
Yes, I check it ___. / Not really.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What will you do this weekend if it rains?" (hint on screen: If it rains, I’ll ___.)
- "What will you do if you finish work early today?" (hint on screen: If I finish early, I’ll ___.)
- "Do you check the weather forecast? When?" (hint on screen: Yes, I check it ___. / Not really.)
- "Do you prefer outdoor or indoor activities?" (hint on screen: I prefer ___ activities. / It depends on the weather.)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Plan B
steps.text: On Saturday morning, the forecast indicated heavy rain. Daniel sent a text: “It’s raining. Plan B!” The rain determined their plan for the day. They met at the city museum. A small café *opened up* there last month, so they had lunch there. Later, the rain stopped, and they *got out* for a short walk. Then Jiwoo told Daniel her big news: she bought her plane ticket to Toronto! “Is it cold there in April?” “Sometimes it’s below zero,” said Daniel. “If that’s *the case*, I’ll bring a warm jacket.” “Good idea. And *bring back* some maple candy for me!”
steps.gloss: indicate 나타내다, 알려 주다 · determine 정하다, 결정하다 · open up (가게가) 새로 문을 열다 · get out 밖으로 나가다 · If that’s the case 그렇다면 · bring back 사 오다 · below zero 영하
questions: Why did they go to the museum?
What does Daniel want from Toronto?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Plan B". Text: "On Saturday morning, the forecast indicated heavy rain. Daniel sent a text: “It’s raining. Plan B!” The rain determined their plan for the day. They met at the city museum. A small café opened up there last month, so they had lunch there. Later, the rain stopped, and they got out for a short walk. Then Jiwoo told Daniel her big news: she bought her plane ticket to Toronto! “Is it cold there in April?” “Sometimes it’s below zero,” said Daniel. “If that’s the case, I’ll bring a warm jacket.” “Good idea. And bring back some maple candy for me!”" Words: indicate 나타내다, 알려 주다 · determine 정하다, 결정하다 · open up (가게가) 새로 문을 열다 · get out 밖으로 나가다 · If that’s the case 그렇다면 · bring back 사 오다 · below zero 영하.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why did they go to the museum?" / "What does Daniel want from Toronto?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

‘Let’s wait and see.’로 상황을 지켜보자고 할 수 있어요.

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "When I was a kid" (어릴 때). Goal: 어릴 때 하던 일을 묻고 말하기. Today's scene: 3월 저녁, 그레이스네 거실. 따뜻한 차를 마시며 그레이스가 오래된 사진 한 장(바닷가에서 노는 어린아이)을 지우에게 보여 주고, 지우가 웃으며 들여다봄(사진·벽에 글자 없이). steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What did you use to do as a kid? / Did you use to ___? / When I was a kid, I used to ___. Table (어릴 때 (used to) → 지금 (현재형)):
- I used to be very shy. → Now I talk to everyone.
- We used to play outside every day. → Now I work inside all day.
- I didn’t use to like vegetables. → Now I love them.
- I used to read comic books. → Now I read the news.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
예전에 자주 했지만 지금은 안 하는 일: I *used to* swim every day.
예전 상태도 말해요: I *used to* be very shy.

*Did* you *use to* play outside? — Yes, I did. / No, I didn’t.
I *didn’t use to* like math. 예전엔 수학을 안 좋아했어요.
did가 과거를 맡으니 use에 d를 붙이지 않아요.
errors: I use to be very shy.
I used to be very shy.
예전 일은 used to. d를 빼지 않아요.
Did you used to play outside?
Did you use to play outside?
When I was kid, I was shy.
When I was a kid, I was shy.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- used to + 동사원형: 예전에 자주 했지만 지금은 안 하는 일: I used to swim every day. / 예전 상태도 말해요: I used to be very shy.
- 묻기·부정은 use to: Did you use to play outside? — Yes, I did. / No, I didn’t. / I didn’t use to like math. 예전엔 수학을 안 좋아했어요. / did가 과거를 맡으니 use에 d를 붙이지 않아요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I use to be very shy. → I used to be very shy. (예전 일은 used to. d를 빼지 않아요.)
- Did you used to play outside? → Did you use to play outside? (did 뒤에는 use(d 없이).)
- I used to playing outside. → I used to play outside. (used to 뒤엔 동사원형.)
- When I was kid, I was shy. → When I was a kid, I was shy. (kid 앞에 a를 빼지 않아요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

묻기·부정은 use to: Did you use to play outside? — Yes, I did. / No, I didn’t.I didn’t use to like math. 예전엔 수학을 안 좋아했어요.did가 과거를 맡으니 use에 d를 붙이지 않아요.

steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "When I was a kid" (어릴 때); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What did you use to do as a kid?" / "When I was a kid, I used to ___." / "Did you use to ___?". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I used to be very shy.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):

steps.title: Grace’s Seaside Town
steps.text: Grace grew up in a small town by the sea. Her elementary school had only forty children, and it still exists today. In third grade, she didn’t like math, *even though* her dad was a math teacher. After school, she was *supposed to* do her homework, but she used to run to the beach. Her mom used to say, “Be home *in time* for dinner!” Last summer, Grace found an old tape from her childhood at her mom’s house. On it, little Grace reads a story: “Once upon a time…”

steps.title: 그때 뭐 하고 있었어요?
steps.goal: 어떤 일이 일어났을 때 하고 있던 일 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 3월 말 오후, 동네 모퉁이 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼이 손으로 머리 감는 시늉을 하며 웃고, 지우도 웃으며 손뼉을 침. 테이블 위에 커피 두 잔(창밖·벽에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "What were you doing?" (그때 뭐 하고 있었어요?). Goal: 어떤 일이 일어났을 때 하고 있던 일 말하기. Today's scene: 3월 말 오후, 동네 모퉁이 카페 창가 자리. 대니얼이 손으로 머리 감는 시늉을 하며 웃고, 지우도 웃으며 손뼉을 침. 테이블 위에 커피 두 잔(창밖·벽에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "What were you doing when ___?".

steps.when: 어떤 일이 일어난 그 순간에 하던 일을 물어요.
steps.extra: What were you doing when the lights went out?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "What were you doing when ___?" (~했을 때 뭐 하고 있었어요?). When to use it: 어떤 일이 일어난 그 순간에 하던 일을 물어요. Note: What were you doing when the lights went out?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I was ___ing when ___.".

steps.when: 하고 있던 일(was + -ing)에 갑자기 일어난 일(과거형)을 이어요.
steps.extra: I was taking a shower when the lights went out.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I was ___ing when ___." (~하고 있는데 ~했어요.). When to use it: 하고 있던 일(was + -ing)에 갑자기 일어난 일(과거형)을 이어요. Note: I was taking a shower when the lights went out.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "What a coincidence!".

steps.when: 우연히 같은 일이 생겼을 때 놀라며 말해요.
steps.extra: I was cooking, too! — What a coincidence!
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "What a coincidence!" (이런 우연이 있나!). When to use it: 우연히 같은 일이 생겼을 때 놀라며 말해요. Note: I was cooking, too! — What a coincidence!
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("The Night the Lights Went Out · 3월 말, 동네 카페에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: The Night the Lights Went Out · 3월 말, 동네 카페에서

lines.en: Jiwoo! The lights went out in our neighborhood last night. Were you at home?
lines.ko: 지우! 어젯밤에 우리 동네 정전됐잖아요. 집에 있었어요?

lines.en: Yes! At about nine, suddenly, everything went dark.
lines.ko: 네! 아홉 시쯤 갑자기 다 깜깜해졌어요.

lines.en: {{What were you doing when}} it happened?
lines.ko: 그때 뭐 하고 있었어요?

lines.en: {{I was}} tak{{ing}} a shower {{when}} the lights went out!
lines.ko: 샤워하고 있는데 불이 나갔어요!

lines.en: No way! I was washing my hair at that moment.
lines.ko: 말도 안 돼! 저는 그 순간에 머리를 감고 있었어요.

lines.en: Really? {{What a coincidence!}} So what did you do?
lines.ko: 정말요? 이런 우연이! 그래서 어떻게 했어요?

lines.en: I walked out very slowly, but I accidentally bumped into the door.
lines.ko: 아주 천천히 걸어 나왔는데, 실수로 문에 쿵 부딪혔어요.

lines.en: Ha! I sat on the floor in my towel. Then my phone rang.
lines.ko: 하하! 저는 수건을 두르고 바닥에 앉아 있었어요. 그때 전화가 울렸어요.

lines.en: Who was calling?
lines.ko: 누가 전화했어요?

lines.en: Grace! She was standing in the hallway with lots of candles.
lines.ko: 그레이스요! 복도에 초를 잔뜩 들고 서 있었어요.

lines.en: That’s funny. In my building, everyone was laughing on the stairs.
lines.ko: 재밌네요. 우리 건물에선 다들 계단에서 웃고 있었어요.

lines.en: The lights came back at ten. I was just about to go to bed!
lines.ko: 열 시에 불이 다시 들어왔어요. 막 자려던 참이었는데!

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "The Night the Lights Went Out · 3월 말, 동네 카페에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Daniel: "Jiwoo! The lights went out in our neighborhood last night. Were you at home?" (지우! 어젯밤에 우리 동네 정전됐잖아요. 집에 있었어요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Yes! At about nine, suddenly, everything went dark." (네! 아홉 시쯤 갑자기 다 깜깜해졌어요.)
3. Daniel: "What were you doing when it happened?" (그때 뭐 하고 있었어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "I was taking a shower when the lights went out!" (샤워하고 있는데 불이 나갔어요!)
5. Daniel: "No way! I was washing my hair at that moment." (말도 안 돼! 저는 그 순간에 머리를 감고 있었어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Really? What a coincidence! So what did you do?" (정말요? 이런 우연이! 그래서 어떻게 했어요?)
7. Daniel: "I walked out very slowly, but I accidentally bumped into the door." (아주 천천히 걸어 나왔는데, 실수로 문에 쿵 부딪혔어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Ha! I sat on the floor in my towel. Then my phone rang." (하하! 저는 수건을 두르고 바닥에 앉아 있었어요. 그때 전화가 울렸어요.)
9. Daniel: "Who was calling?" (누가 전화했어요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Grace! She was standing in the hallway with lots of candles." (그레이스요! 복도에 초를 잔뜩 들고 서 있었어요.)
11. Daniel: "That’s funny. In my building, everyone was laughing on the stairs." (재밌네요. 우리 건물에선 다들 계단에서 웃고 있었어요.)
12. Jiwoo: "The lights came back at ten. I was just about to go to bed!" (열 시에 불이 다시 들어왔어요. 막 자려던 참이었는데!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

3. Grace called Jiwoo.
The scene they are about:
1. Daniel: "Jiwoo! The lights went out in our neighborhood last night. Were you at home?" (지우! 어젯밤에 우리 동네 정전됐잖아요. 집에 있었어요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Yes! At about nine, suddenly, everything went dark." (네! 아홉 시쯤 갑자기 다 깜깜해졌어요.)
3. Daniel: "What were you doing when it happened?" (그때 뭐 하고 있었어요?)
4. Jiwoo: "I was taking a shower when the lights went out!" (샤워하고 있는데 불이 나갔어요!)
5. Daniel: "No way! I was washing my hair at that moment." (말도 안 돼! 저는 그 순간에 머리를 감고 있었어요.)
6. Jiwoo: "Really? What a coincidence! So what did you do?" (정말요? 이런 우연이! 그래서 어떻게 했어요?)
7. Daniel: "I walked out very slowly, but I accidentally bumped into the door." (아주 천천히 걸어 나왔는데, 실수로 문에 쿵 부딪혔어요.)
8. Jiwoo: "Ha! I sat on the floor in my towel. Then my phone rang." (하하! 저는 수건을 두르고 바닥에 앉아 있었어요. 그때 전화가 울렸어요.)
9. Daniel: "Who was calling?" (누가 전화했어요?)
10. Jiwoo: "Grace! She was standing in the hallway with lots of candles." (그레이스요! 복도에 초를 잔뜩 들고 서 있었어요.)
11. Daniel: "That’s funny. In my building, everyone was laughing on the stairs." (재밌네요. 우리 건물에선 다들 계단에서 웃고 있었어요.)
12. Jiwoo: "The lights came back at ten. I was just about to go to bed!" (열 시에 불이 다시 들어왔어요. 막 자려던 참이었는데!)
Before you judge an answer, check the scene lines carefully: who said what. Ask one statement at a time: read it yourself and ask True or false?. Accept true/false, yes/no, or Korean (맞아요/틀려요). Say whether they are right and point to the line that shows it in a few words, also when they are right. Do all 3 statements, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a table of useful sentences for real situations.

head: 하고 있던 일 (was + -ing)
갑자기 일어난 일 (과거형)
steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: What were you doing when ___? / I was ___ing when ___. Table (하고 있던 일 (was + -ing) → 갑자기 일어난 일 (과거형)):
- I was cooking → when the phone rang.
- I was walking home → when it started to rain.
- We were watching TV → when the lights went out.
- She was taking a shower → when you called.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
그때 하고 있던 일: I *was* cook*ing*. 요리하고 있었어요.
I·he·she·it → *was* / you·we·they → *were*
물을 때: *Were* you sleeping? — Yes, I was. / No, I wasn’t.

길게 하던 일 + 짧게 일어난 일:
I was cooking *when* the phone rang.
The phone rang *while* I was cooking.
while 뒤엔 주로 하고 있던 일(was + -ing)이 와요.
errors: I was cooking when the phone was ring.
I was cooking when the phone rang.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- was/were + -ing (과거진행형): 그때 하고 있던 일: I was cooking. 요리하고 있었어요. / I·he·she·it → was / you·we·they → were / 물을 때: Were you sleeping? — Yes, I was. / No, I wasn’t.
- when · while: 길게 하던 일 + 짧게 일어난 일: / I was cooking when the phone rang. / The phone rang while I was cooking. / while 뒤엔 주로 하고 있던 일(was + -ing)이 와요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I was take a shower. → I was taking a shower. (was 뒤엔 -ing.)
- What you were doing? → What were you doing? (물을 땐 were를 you 앞으로.)
- They was laughing. → They were laughing. (they·we·you는 were.)
- I was cooking when the phone was ring. → I was cooking when the phone rang. (갑자기 일어난 일은 과거형(rang).)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: was/were + -ing (과거진행형): 그때 하고 있던 일: I was cooking. 요리하고 있었어요.I·he·she·it → was / you·we·they → were물을 때: Were you sleeping? — Yes, I was. / No, I wasn’t.
when · while: 길게 하던 일 + 짧게 일어난 일:I was cooking when the phone rang.The phone rang while I was cooking.while 뒤엔 주로 하고 있던 일(was + -ing)이 와요.
mistakes: I was take a shower. → I was taking a shower.
What you were doing? → What were you doing?
They was laughing. → They were laughing.
I was cooking when the phone was ring. → I was cooking when the phone rang.

steps.note: 예) cook / the phone rang → What were you doing when the phone rang? — I was cooking when the phone rang.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) cook / the phone rang → What were you doing when the phone rang? — I was cooking when the phone rang. Items (situation → model answer): cook → the phone rang | walk home → it started to rain | watch TV → the lights went out | sleep → you called.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "What were you doing?" (그때 뭐 하고 있었어요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "What were you doing when ___?" / "I was ___ing when ___." / "What a coincidence!". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

groups: I was taking a shower when you called.
The phone rang while I was cooking.
Sorry, I was in a meeting.
I was just about to call you.
steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 하고 있던 일 말하기: "I was taking a shower when you called." (전화했을 때 샤워하고 있었어요., 보통); "The phone rang while I was cooking." (요리하는 동안 전화가 울렸어요., 보통); "I was walking home." (집에 걸어가고 있었어요., 보통); "Were you sleeping?" (자고 있었어요?, 친근)
- 전화를 못 받았을 때: "Sorry, I was in a meeting." (미안해요, 회의 중이었어요., 정중); "I was just about to call you." (막 전화하려던 참이었어요., 보통)
- 그때 일 이야기하기: "Suddenly, the lights went out." (갑자기 불이 나갔어요., 보통); "Everyone was laughing." (다들 웃고 있었어요., 보통); "That’s funny." (재밌네요., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: when · while · during

I was cooking *when* the phone rang.
The phone rang *while* I was cooking.
*during* + 명사: *during* the blackout 정전 동안 · during the meeting 회의 동안
정전 이야기 낱말

The lights *went out*. 불이 나갔어요. · The lights *came back*. 불이 다시 들어왔어요.
a blackout 정전 · *knock* on the door 문을 두드리다
*enter* the room 방에 들어가다
steps.blank:
A: What ___ you doing when the lights went out?   B: I was ___ a shower!
A: Me too! What a ___!   B: Then my phone rang ___ I was in the dark.
낱말 상자: were · taking · coincidence · while
steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- when · while · during: I was cooking when the phone rang. / The phone rang while I was cooking. / during + 명사: during the blackout 정전 동안 · during the meeting 회의 동안
- 정전 이야기 낱말: The lights went out. 불이 나갔어요. · The lights came back. 불이 다시 들어왔어요. / a blackout 정전 · knock on the door 문을 두드리다 / enter the room 방에 들어가다
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: What ___ you doing when the lights went out? B: I was ___ a shower! / A: Me too! What a ___! B: Then my phone rang ___ I was in the dark. / 낱말 상자: were · taking · coincidence · while
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: laugh (웃다), cry (울다), dark (어두운, 깜깜한), stairs (계단), bump (부딪히다), knock (두드리다), enter (들어가다), ambulance (구급차), shower (샤워), ring ((전화가) 울리다), light (불, 전등(앞에서는 ‘가벼운’)), ran (달렸다(run의 과거)).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: I accidentally bumped into the door.
Sorry, I was in a meeting.
My phone fell on the floor.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: while (~하는 동안) — "while I was cooking"; when (~할 때) — "when the lights went out"; coincidence (우연) — "What a coincidence!"; during (~ 동안(+명사)) — "during the meeting"; accidentally (실수로, 우연히) — "I accidentally bumped into the door."; suddenly (갑자기) — "Suddenly, everything went dark."; happen ((일이) 일어나다) — "What happened?"; meeting (회의) — "Sorry, I was in a meeting."; moment (순간) — "at that moment"; fell (떨어졌다(fall의 과거)) — "My phone fell on the floor.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: What were you doing at nine last night?
What were you doing this morning at eight?
I was ___ing. / I was on my way to ___.
Your phone rang, but you didn’t answer. What do you say later?
Sorry, I was in a meeting. / I was ___ing.
Tell me about a funny coincidence.
I was ___ing when ___. What a coincidence!
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "What were you doing at nine last night?" (hint on screen: I was ___ing.)
- "What were you doing this morning at eight?" (hint on screen: I was ___ing. / I was on my way to ___.)
- "Your phone rang, but you didn’t answer. What do you say later?" (hint on screen: Sorry, I was in a meeting. / I was ___ing.)
- "Tell me about a funny coincidence." (hint on screen: I was ___ing when ___. What a coincidence!)
- "Ask me about last night." (hint on screen: What were you doing at ___?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.
questions: What were you doing at nine last night?
What were you doing this morning at eight?
Your phone rang, but you didn’t answer. What do you say later?
Tell me about a funny coincidence.
Ask me about last night.

steps.title: Our Building in the Dark
steps.text: Last night at nine, the lights went out in the whole neighborhood. During the blackout, the elevator stopped, so people used the stairs. Ben was walking home when it happened. A little boy on the third floor was crying, so Ben acted fast. He told funny stories, and soon the boy was laughing. Then Grace *showed up* with *lots of* candles. A worker entered the building. “We’re fixing a cable *at the moment*,” he said. Jiwoo saw a small movement near the stairs. It was a neighbor’s cat! At ten, the lights came back.
steps.gloss: blackout 정전 · during ~ 동안 · act 행동하다 · show up 나타나다 · lots of 많은 · enter 들어오다 · at the moment 지금 · movement 움직임
questions: What was Ben doing when the lights went out?
Who showed up with lots of candles?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "Our Building in the Dark". Text: "Last night at nine, the lights went out in the whole neighborhood. During the blackout, the elevator stopped, so people used the stairs. Ben was walking home when it happened. A little boy on the third floor was crying, so Ben acted fast. He told funny stories, and soon the boy was laughing. Then Grace showed up with lots of candles. A worker entered the building. “We’re fixing a cable at the moment,” he said. Jiwoo saw a small movement near the stairs. It was a neighbor’s cat! At ten, the lights came back." Words: blackout 정전 · during ~ 동안 · act 행동하다 · show up 나타나다 · lots of 많은 · enter 들어오다 · at the moment 지금 · movement 움직임.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What was Ben doing when the lights went out?" / "Who showed up with lots of candles?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘What were you doing when ___?’로 그때 하던 일을 물을 수 있어요.
‘I was ___ing when ___.’로 하고 있던 일과 일어난 일을 함께 말할 수 있어요.
‘What a coincidence!’로 우연히 같은 일이 생겼을 때 반응할 수 있어요.
steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘What were you doing when ___?’로 그때 하던 일을 물을 수 있어요.
- ‘I was ___ing when ___.’로 하고 있던 일과 일어난 일을 함께 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘What a coincidence!’로 우연히 같은 일이 생겼을 때 반응할 수 있어요.
Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

lessons.title: 해 본 적 있어요?

steps.title: 해 본 적 있어요?
steps.goal: 경험을 묻고 해 봤다·안 해 봤다고 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 초 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당 창가 자리. 창밖에 벚꽃이 피어 있고, 마야가 휴대폰 속 호숫가 사진을 보여 주며 웃고, 지우가 눈을 크게 뜨고 바라봄
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Have you ever been abroad?" (해 본 적 있어요?). Goal: 경험을 묻고 해 봤다·안 해 봤다고 말하기. Today's scene: 4월 초 평일 점심, 회사 근처 식당 창가 자리. 창밖에 벚꽃이 피어 있고, 마야가 휴대폰 속 호숫가 사진을 보여 주며 웃고, 지우가 눈을 크게 뜨고 바라봄. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Have you ever tried ___?".

steps.when: 살면서 한 번이라도 해 봤는지(경험) 물을 때 써요. ever는 ‘한 번이라도’.
steps.extra: Have you ever tried raw fish?
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Have you ever tried ___?" (~해 본 적 있어요?). When to use it: 살면서 한 번이라도 해 봤는지(경험) 물을 때 써요. ever는 ‘한 번이라도’. Note: Have you ever tried raw fish?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "Yes, I have.".

steps.when: ‘Have you ~?’로 물으면 have로 짧게 대답해요.
steps.extra: A: Have you ever been abroad? B: Yes, I have.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "Yes, I have." (네, 해 봤어요.). When to use it: ‘Have you ~?’로 물으면 have로 짧게 대답해요. Note: A: Have you ever been abroad? B: Yes, I have.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "No, I’ve never tried ___.".

steps.ko: 아뇨, ~ 한 번도 안 해 봤어요.
steps.when: never는 ‘한 번도 ~ 안’. I’ve는 I have를 줄인 말이에요.
steps.extra: No, I’ve never tried skydiving.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "No, I’ve never tried ___." (아뇨, ~ 한 번도 안 해 봤어요.). When to use it: never는 ‘한 번도 ~ 안’. I’ve는 I have를 줄인 말이에요. Note: No, I’ve never tried skydiving.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("My First Trip Abroad · 4월 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.title: My First Trip Abroad · 4월 점심, 회사 근처 식당에서

lines.en: Jiwoo, only three weeks till Toronto! Are you excited?
lines.ko: 지우 씨, 토론토까지 3주밖에 안 남았네요! 신나요?

lines.en: Yes, but I’m a little nervous. I’ve never been abroad.
lines.ko: 네, 그런데 좀 떨려요. 해외에 한 번도 안 가 봤거든요.

lines.en: Really? Your first trip abroad? You’ve got this! And Chloe will be with you.
lines.ko: 정말요? 첫 해외여행이에요? 잘할 거예요! 그리고 클로이가 같이 있잖아요.

lines.en: That’s true. Maya, have you ever been to Toronto?
lines.ko: 맞아요. 마야는 토론토에 가 본 적 있어요?

lines.en: {{Yes, I have.}} I’ve been to Toronto twice.
lines.ko: 네, 가 봤어요. 토론토에 두 번 가 봤어요.

lines.en: Wow. How was it?
lines.ko: 와. 어땠어요?

lines.en: It was amazing. Oh, {{have you ever tried}} maple taffy?
lines.ko: 정말 좋았어요. 아, 메이플 태피 먹어 본 적 있어요?

lines.en: {{No, I’ve never tried}} it. What’s it like?
lines.ko: 아뇨, 한 번도 안 먹어 봤어요. 어떤 거예요?

lines.en: It’s hot maple syrup on cold snow. A little strange, but so good! You should try it.
lines.ko: 뜨거운 메이플 시럽을 차가운 눈 위에 부은 거예요. 좀 이상한데 정말 맛있어요! 꼭 먹어 봐요.

lines.en: I will! You try so many new things, Maya. Have you ever tried skydiving?
lines.ko: 그럴게요! 마야는 새로운 걸 정말 많이 해 보잖아요. 스카이다이빙 해 본 적 있어요?

lines.en: Once, a long time ago. It was scary but amazing! What about you?
lines.ko: 한 번요, 오래전에요. 무서웠지만 정말 멋졌어요! 지우 씨는요?

lines.en: Never in my life! But I’d like to try it someday… maybe.
lines.ko: 평생 한 번도 없죠! 그래도 언젠가 해 보고 싶어요… 아마도요.

steps.teach:

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Have you ever tried ___? / Yes, I have. / No, I’ve never tried ___. Table (해 볼 것 (Have you ever tried …?) → 해 봤어요):
- raw fish 회 → Yes, I have. It was great.
- skydiving 스카이다이빙 → Yes, once. It was amazing!
- yoga 요가 → Yes, I have. I like it.
- snowboarding 스노보드 → Yes, twice. It was hard!
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items: have + p.p. — 해 본 적 있어요

지금까지 살면서 해 본 일(경험)을 말해요.
I *have tried* it. = *I’ve* tried it. 해 봤어요.
물을 때: *Have* you *ever tried* it? 대답: Yes, I have. / No, I haven’t.
ever 한 번이라도 · never 한 번도 ~ 안

규칙: try → *tried* · visit → *visited* (과거형과 같아요)
불규칙: be → *been* · eat → *eaten* · see → *seen*
I’ve *been* to Busan. 부산에 가 봤어요.
errors: Have you ever try raw fish?

경험을 물을 때는 Have you ever + p.p.예요.
I have been to Toronto last year.
I went to Toronto last year.
last year처럼 때가 분명하면 과거형으로 말해요.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- have + p.p. — 해 본 적 있어요: 지금까지 살면서 해 본 일(경험)을 말해요. / I have tried it. = I’ve tried it. 해 봤어요. / 물을 때: Have you ever tried it? 대답: Yes, I have. / No, I haven’t. / ever 한 번이라도 · never 한 번도 ~ 안
- p.p.(과거분사) 모양: 규칙: try → tried · visit → visited (과거형과 같아요) / 불규칙: be → been · eat → eaten · see → seen / I’ve been to Busan. 부산에 가 봤어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- Have you ever try raw fish? → Have you ever tried raw fish? (have 뒤에는 p.p.(tried)를 써요.)
- Did you ever been abroad? → Have you ever been abroad? (경험을 물을 때는 Have you ever + p.p.예요.)
- I’ve been to abroad. → I’ve been abroad. (abroad 앞에는 to를 쓰지 않아요.)
- I have been to Toronto last year. → I went to Toronto last year. (last year처럼 때가 분명하면 과거형으로 말해요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.

steps.title: Maya’s Soccer League
steps.text: Maya plays in a soccer *league* for office workers. She started as an adult. “I’ve never been a real athlete,” she says, “but I love my team.” Every April, the league has a big *tournament*, so Maya *associates* spring *with* soccer. Last year, her team *went through* four hard games. In the final, Maya made one attempt at a goal, but she missed. *In addition*, it started to rain! Still, it was an amazing experience. *As far as* she knows, it was the team’s best year. This year, Jiwoo will miss it. “Send me a photo of the lake when you get there!” says Maya.

steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Have you packed yet?" (벌써 했어요?). Goal: 이미 했는지, 아직인지 묻고 답하기. Today's scene: 4월 평일 저녁, 아파트 5층 복도. 퇴근한 지우가 가방을 멘 채 지친 얼굴로 서 있고, 옆집 그레이스가 문 앞에서 웃으며 손가락으로 하나씩 세어 가며 이야기함. 지우 집 문 옆 창가에 화분 몇 개가 보임. steps.when: 해야 할 일을 했는지 물을 때 써요. yet은 문장 맨 끝에 와요.

steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Have you ___ yet?" (벌써 ~했어요? / ~했어요?). When to use it: 해야 할 일을 했는지 물을 때 써요. yet은 문장 맨 끝에 와요. Note: Have you packed yet? · Have you eaten yet?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I’ve just ___.".

steps.when: 바로 조금 전에 끝낸 일을 말해요. just는 have와 p.p. 사이에 넣어요.

steps.teach:

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Have you ___ yet? / Yes, I’ve just ___. / Not yet. Table (할 일 (Have you … yet?) → 했어요 (just · already)):
- packed 짐을 쌌다 → Yes, I’ve just packed.
- eaten 먹었다 → Yes, I’ve already eaten.
- booked a hotel 호텔을 예약했다 → Yes, I’ve just booked one.
- finished the report 보고서를 끝냈다 → Yes, I’ve already finished it.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.

items:
*just* 방금 · *already* 벌써 — have와 p.p. 사이에

*yet* (물을 때) 벌써 · (안 했을 때) 아직 — 문장 끝에
Have you eaten *yet*? · I haven’t finished it *yet*.

I have → *I’ve* · she has → *she’s* · have not → *haven’t*
do → *done* · hear → *heard* · lose → *lost* · leave → *left*

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:

- 줄임말과 p.p. 더 보기: I have → I’ve · she has → she’s · have not → haven’t / do → done · hear → heard · lose → lost · leave → left / 3-15의 been·eaten·seen도 같은 p.p.예요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’ve already eat. → I’ve already eaten. (have 뒤에는 p.p.(eaten)를 써요.)
- I’ve just arrived yesterday. → I arrived yesterday. (yesterday처럼 지난 때를 말하면 과거형으로 말해요.)
- Have you finished yet it? → Have you finished it yet? (yet은 문장 맨 끝에 와요.)
- Yes, I’ve finished it yet. → Yes, I’ve already finished it. (했다고 말할 때 ‘벌써’는 already. yet은 묻거나 안 했을 때 써요.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

steps.note: 예) eaten lunch / 방금 했어요 → Have you eaten lunch yet? — Yes, I’ve just eaten. · 아직이요 → Not yet.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) eaten lunch / 방금 했어요 → Have you eaten lunch yet? — Yes, I’ve just eaten. · 아직이요 → Not yet. Items (situation → model answer): eaten lunch → 방금 했어요 | packed → 아직이요 | booked a hotel → 벌써 했어요 | heard the news → 아직이요.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "Have you packed yet?" (벌써 했어요?); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Have you ___ yet?" / "I’ve just ___." / "Not yet.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 했다고 말하기: "I’ve already done it." (그건 벌써 했어요., 보통); "I’ve just arrived." (방금 도착했어요., 보통); "I’ve lost my wallet." (지갑을 잃어버렸어요., 보통); "She’s already left." (그분은 벌써 떠났어요., 보통)
- 아직이라고 말하기: "I haven’t finished it yet." (아직 다 못 끝냈어요., 보통); "I’ve been so busy." (요즘 정말 바빴어요., 친근)
- 묻고 소식 나누기: "Have you eaten yet?" (밥 먹었어요?, 친근); "Have you heard the news?" (그 소식 들었어요?, 보통); "Not yet, what is it?" (아직이요, 뭔데요?, 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Have you eaten dinner yet?" (hint on screen: Yes, I’ve already eaten. / Not yet.)
- "Have you finished your work for today?" (hint on screen: Yes, I’ve just finished. / Not yet.)
- "Have you heard any good news recently?" (hint on screen: Yes! I’ve just heard ___. / Not yet.)

- "Ask me a question with ‘yet’." (hint on screen: Have you ___ yet?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Grace’s Checklist
steps.text: Jiwoo has been busy *recently*, so Grace made her a checklist. “Treat it *as though* it’s a game,” said Grace. “Finish one thing, then *move on* to the next.” Jiwoo has already done three things. She has booked a hotel, *signed up* for travel insurance, and *topped up* her travel card. But she hasn’t packed yet. Her room isn’t very *tidy*, so she *searched* the floor for her suitcase. At last, she *stood up*. There it was, on top of the closet! The last line says, “After the trip, *unpack* and rest.” Grace says, “Take small steps. You’ll feel calmer and be ready on time.”
steps.gloss: checklist 할 일 목록 · as though 마치 ~인 것처럼 · move on 넘어가다 · travel insurance 여행자 보험 · stand up 일어서다 · closet 붙박이장 · (참고) maintain 유지하다 — maintain a calm mind · thus 그래서(글에서 쓰는 말)
questions: What has Jiwoo already done?
Where was her suitcase?

steps.title: 공항에서
steps.title_en: I’d like a window seat, please.
steps.goal: 탑승 수속에서 원하는 자리를 말하고 필요한 곳을 묻기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 말 아침, 인천공항 항공사 카운터. 지우와 클로이가 여행 가방을 저울 위에 올려놓고 여권을 내밀고, 카운터 직원(조연)이 웃으며 받음. 큰 유리창 밖으로 비행기가 보임
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "I’d like a window seat, please." (공항에서). Goal: 탑승 수속에서 원하는 자리를 말하고 필요한 곳을 묻기. Today's scene: 4월 말 아침, 인천공항 항공사 카운터. 지우와 클로이가 여행 가방을 저울 위에 올려놓고 여권을 내밀고, 카운터 직원(조연)이 웃으며 받음. 큰 유리창 밖으로 비행기가 보임. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I’d like a window seat, please.".

steps.en: I’d like a window seat, please.

steps.extra: I’d like an aisle seat, please.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I’d like a window seat, please." (창가 자리로 주세요.). When to use it: 탑승 수속 때 원하는 자리를 공손하게 말해요. I’d like = I would like. Note: I’d like an aisle seat, please.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "How long is the flight?".

Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

Expression 3 of 3: "Where can I find ___?" (~는 어디에 있어요?). When to use it: 공항·가게에서 찾는 곳을 물어요. Note: Where can I find the duty-free shops?
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("At the Check-in Counter · 4월 말 아침, 인천공항에서") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.teach:
The app has just played this scene, "At the Check-in Counter · 4월 말 아침, 인천공항에서", in the characters' own voices. The learner heard it and sees it on screen:
1. Staff: "Good morning. Can I see your passport, please? Any bags to check in?" (안녕하세요. 여권 보여 주시겠어요? 부칠 짐 있으세요?)
2. Jiwoo: "Here you are. Just one. And I’d like a window seat, please." (여기요. 하나요. 그리고 창가 자리로 주세요.)
3. Chloe: "Ooh, that sounded so natural! An aisle seat for me, please. Can we sit together?" (오, 정말 자연스러웠어요! 저는 통로 쪽 자리로 주세요. 같이 앉을 수 있어요?)
4. Staff: "Sure. You’re in Row 32, A and C. The middle seat is empty." (그럼요. 32열 A석과 C석이에요. 가운데 자리는 비어 있어요.)
5. Jiwoo: "Great! How long is the flight?" (잘됐다! 비행시간이 얼마나 돼요?)
6. Staff: "About thirteen hours. Your gate is 23." (13시간쯤이요. 게이트는 23번입니다.)
7. Chloe: "Is the flight on time?" (비행기는 제시간에 떠요?)
8. Staff: "Sorry, it’s been delayed thirty minutes. Boarding starts at 10:10." (죄송합니다. 30분 지연됐어요. 탑승은 10시 10분에 시작해요.)
9. Jiwoo: "That’s okay. Where can I find the duty-free shops?" (괜찮아요. 면세점은 어디에 있어요?)
10. Staff: "After security. There are restrooms throughout the airport, too." (보안 검색 뒤에요. 화장실은 공항 곳곳에 있어요.)
11. Chloe: "Thanks! Come on, Jiwoo. Toronto, here we come!" (고마워요! 가요, 지우 씨. 토론토, 우리가 간다!)
Talk about it like a person: a short natural reaction, then one simple question about what happened (the answer is in the lines above). React to their answer; if it is not right, point kindly to the line that shows it. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): role reading of that scene.

steps.teach:
Role reading of the same scene. The learner is Jiwoo; you read the lines of Staff, Chloe exactly as written, word for word. Never change, add or skip a line, and never read the learner's lines for them first.
1. Staff (you): "Good morning. Can I see your passport, please? Any bags to check in?" (안녕하세요. 여권 보여 주시겠어요? 부칠 짐 있으세요?)
2. Jiwoo (learner): "Here you are. Just one. And I’d like a window seat, please." (여기요. 하나요. 그리고 창가 자리로 주세요.)
3. Chloe (you): "Ooh, that sounded so natural! An aisle seat for me, please. Can we sit together?" (오, 정말 자연스러웠어요! 저는 통로 쪽 자리로 주세요. 같이 앉을 수 있어요?)
4. Staff (you): "Sure. You’re in Row 32, A and C. The middle seat is empty." (그럼요. 32열 A석과 C석이에요. 가운데 자리는 비어 있어요.)
5. Jiwoo (learner): "Great! How long is the flight?" (잘됐다! 비행시간이 얼마나 돼요?)
6. Staff (you): "About thirteen hours. Your gate is 23." (13시간쯤이요. 게이트는 23번입니다.)
7. Chloe (you): "Is the flight on time?" (비행기는 제시간에 떠요?)
8. Staff (you): "Sorry, it’s been delayed thirty minutes. Boarding starts at 10:10." (죄송합니다. 30분 지연됐어요. 탑승은 10시 10분에 시작해요.)
9. Jiwoo (learner): "That’s okay. Where can I find the duty-free shops?" (괜찮아요. 면세점은 어디에 있어요?)
10. Staff (you): "After security. There are restrooms throughout the airport, too." (보안 검색 뒤에요. 화장실은 공항 곳곳에 있어요.)
11. Chloe (you): "Thanks! Come on, Jiwoo. Toronto, here we come!" (고마워요! 가요, 지우 씨. 토론토, 우리가 간다!)
First say in one short sentence that they will be Jiwoo and you will read Staff and Chloe. Then go in order, one line at a time: call highlight_line with the line number before each line, read your line, and for the learner's line just wait for them to say it. If they say only part of it, say that line once and let them try once more, then go on. After the last line, give one short warm comment on how they did, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick true/false check about the scene.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- How long ~? 얼마나 오래: How long is the flight? 비행시간이 얼마나 돼요? / 대답: (It’s) about thirteen hours. 13시간쯤이요. / How long does it take? 얼마나 걸려요?
- Where can I find ~? · I’d like ~: Where can I find Gate 23? 23번 게이트는 어디 있어요? / 짧게: Where’s the restroom? 화장실 어디예요? / 공손한 부탁: I’d like a window seat.
Common mistakes on screen:
- I’d like window seat, please. → I’d like a window seat, please. (seat 앞에 a를 넣어요.)
- How long the flight is? → How long is the flight? (물을 때는 is를 주어 앞으로.)
- Where can I find restroom? → Where can I find the restroom? (restroom 앞에 the(또는 a)를 넣어요.)
- The flight has delayed. → The flight has been delayed. (비행기는 ‘지연된’ 것이라 has been delayed.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.

cards: I’d like a window seat, please.
steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "I’d like a window seat, please." (공항에서); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I’d like a window seat, please." / "How long is the flight?" / "Where can I find ___?". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 탑승 수속: "Can I see your passport?" (여권 보여 주시겠어요?, 정중); "Here you are." (여기요., 보통); "Any bags to check in?" (부칠 짐 있으세요?, 보통); "Just one." (하나요., 보통)
- 게이트와 시간: "Your gate is ___." (게이트는 ~번이에요., 정중); "Boarding starts at ___." (탑승은 ~시에 시작해요., 정중); "Is the flight on time?" (비행기가 제시간에 떠요?, 보통); "It’s been delayed." (지연됐어요., 보통)
- 묻고 부탁하기: "Where’s the restroom?" (화장실이 어디예요?, 보통); "Can we sit together?" (같이 앉을 수 있어요?, 정중)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Picture words on screen. New: airport (공항), plane (비행기), passport (여권), boarding pass (탑승권), seat (자리, 좌석), aisle (통로), gate (탑승구, 게이트), security (보안 검색(대)), luggage ((여행) 짐), officer ((출입국) 직원, 관리), border (국경, 출입국 심사대), restroom (화장실).

What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: flight (비행, 항공편) — "How long is the flight?"; board ((비행기에) 타다) — "Please board now."; international (국제의) — "an international flight"; duty (세금(관세)) — "a duty-free shop 면세점"; aircraft (항공기) — "The aircraft is ready."; ticket (표) — "a plane ticket"; window (창문) — "a window seat"; check ((짐을) 부치다(앞에서는 ‘확인하다, 알아보다’)) — "Any bags to check in?"; delay (늦어짐, 지연; 늦추다) — "The flight has been delayed.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. steps.title: Time Travel
steps.text: After check-in at the airline counter, Jiwoo and Chloe go through security. A guard scans their bags. Oops! Jiwoo has a big bottle of water in her carry-on bag. Carry-on liquids must be in containers of 100 ml or less! At the gate, there’s an announcement, “Passengers for Toronto, please board now.” On the plane, the pilot says hello, and Jiwoo *finds herself* smiling. Her first international flight! Chloe watches Korean dramas throughout the flight. At the border, an officer asks, “Anything to declare?” “No, nothing.” They left Seoul in the morning, and it’s still morning in Toronto! “Don’t sleep now,” says Chloe. “*As long as* you stay awake till tonight, you’ll be fine.”
steps.gloss: airline 항공사 · guard 요원, 경비원 · scan (기계로) 검사하다 · liquid 액체 · announcement 안내 방송 · find oneself 어느새 ~하고 있다 · throughout ~ 내내 · declare (세관에) 신고하다 · as long as ~하기만 하면
questions: What does Chloe do throughout the flight?
Is it morning or night in Toronto?

steps.title: 호텔 체크인
steps.title_en: I have a reservation under Kim Jiwoo.
steps.goal: 예약을 확인하고 체크아웃·아침 식사를 묻기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 말 저녁, 토론토의 작은 호텔 로비 프런트. 여행 가방 옆에서 지우가 종이 양식을 쓰고, 클로이가 옆에서 손가락으로 칸을 가리켜 주고, 프런트 직원(조연)이 카드 키를 내밂
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "I have a reservation under Kim Jiwoo." (호텔 체크인). Goal: 예약을 확인하고 체크아웃·아침 식사를 묻기. Today's scene: 4월 말 저녁, 토론토의 작은 호텔 로비 프런트. 여행 가방 옆에서 지우가 종이 양식을 쓰고, 클로이가 옆에서 손가락으로 칸을 가리켜 주고, 프런트 직원(조연)이 카드 키를 내밂. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "I have a reservation under ___.".

steps.when: 호텔·식당에서 예약을 확인할 때 써요. under 뒤에 *이름*.
steps.extra: I have a reservation under Kim Jiwoo.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "I have a reservation under ___." (~ 이름으로 예약했어요.). When to use it: 호텔·식당에서 예약을 확인할 때 써요. under 뒤에 이름. Note: I have a reservation under Kim Jiwoo.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "What time is check-out?".

steps.when: 방을 비워야 하는 시간을 물어요.
steps.extra: 대답: It’s at eleven.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: I have a reservation under ___. / What time is check-out? / Is ___ included? Table (포함인지 묻기 (Is … included?) → 대답):
- breakfast 아침 식사 → Yes, it is.
- Wi-Fi 와이파이 → Yes, it’s free.
- parking 주차 → No. It’s $20 a night.
- the minibar 미니바 → No, it’s extra. 따로 내요.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- under + 이름 · for + 기간: I have a reservation under Kim Jiwoo. 김지우 이름으로 예약했어요. / a room for three nights 3박 · For how many nights? 몇 박이에요? / 영어권에서는 보통 이름을 먼저 말해요: Jiwoo Kim.
- Is ___ included? · What time ~?: Is breakfast included? 아침 포함돼요? / 대답: Yes, it is. · No, it’s extra. 따로 내요. / ‘몇 시’는 What time: What time is check-out? / check-in 체크인 ↔ check-out 체크아웃
Common mistakes on screen:
- I have a reservation in Kim Jiwoo. → I have a reservation under Kim Jiwoo. (예약자 이름 앞에는 under.)
- Is breakfast include? → Is breakfast included? (‘포함된’은 included.)
- I have reservation under Kim Jiwoo. → I have a reservation under Kim Jiwoo. (reservation 앞에 a를 넣어요.)
- Three night. → Three nights. (둘 이상이면 nights.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "I have a reservation under ___." / "What time is check-out?" / "Is breakfast included?". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.

steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "I’m at the front desk. Good evening! Can I help you?" (hint on screen: Hi. I have a reservation under ___.)
- "For how many nights?" (hint on screen: ___ nights. Is breakfast included?)
- "Which do you like, a big hotel or a small hotel? Why?" (hint on screen: I like ___ hotels because ___.)
- "What do you usually ask at a hotel front desk?" (hint on screen: What time is check-out? / Is there Wi-Fi?)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: Jiwoo’s Little Hotel
steps.text: Chloe’s parents’ house is full this week. Some relations are visiting. So Jiwoo is staying at a small hotel near them. It has two wings, and her single room is in the new wing. In the lobby, a flight crew is checking in, too. Her room has soft towels and a little minibar. A small juice is four dollars and fifty cents! From her window, she can see a row of old houses. Chloe’s parents live on that street! *By the time* Jiwoo unpacks, it’s nine o’clock. Tomorrow at eight, Chloe is going to meet her *in front of* the hotel.
steps.gloss: relation 친척 · wing (건물의) 동 · crew 승무원 · row 줄 · by the time ~할 때쯤 · unpack 짐을 풀다 · in front of ~ 앞에
questions: Why is Jiwoo staying at a hotel?
What can Jiwoo see from her window?

Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "Why is Jiwoo staying at a hotel?" / "What can Jiwoo see from her window?".
