steps.title: 문제가 있어요
steps.goal: 문제를 설명하고 사과에 답하기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 말 아침, 토론토의 작은 호텔 프런트. 실내인데 두꺼운 스웨터를 입은 지우가 프런트 직원에게 방 열쇠 카드를 보이며 설명하고, 옆에서 클로이가 고개를 끄덕임
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "It doesn’t work." (문제가 있어요). Goal: 문제를 설명하고 사과에 답하기. Today's scene: 4월 말 아침, 토론토의 작은 호텔 프런트. 실내인데 두꺼운 스웨터를 입은 지우가 프런트 직원에게 방 열쇠 카드를 보이며 설명하고, 옆에서 클로이가 고개를 끄덕임. Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "There’s a problem with my ___.".

steps.when: 호텔·가게에서 무엇에 문제가 있는지 먼저 말할 때 써요.
steps.extra: There’s a problem with my room. · There’s a problem with my heater.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "There’s a problem with my ___." (제 ~에 문제가 있어요.). When to use it: 호텔·가게에서 무엇에 문제가 있는지 먼저 말할 때 써요. Note: There’s a problem with my room. · There’s a problem with my heater.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "It doesn’t work.".

steps.when: 기계나 물건이 안 될 때 써요. it 뒤에는 *doesn’t* + 동사원형.
steps.extra: The heater doesn’t work. · The light doesn’t work.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "It doesn’t work." (작동이 안 돼요.). When to use it: 기계나 물건이 안 될 때 써요. it 뒤에는 doesn’t + 동사원형. Note: The heater doesn’t work. · The light doesn’t work.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "I’m sorry about that.".

steps.when: 직원이 자기 쪽 문제를 사과할 때 써요.
steps.extra: 대답: That’s all right. (괜찮아요)
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "I’m sorry about that." (그 점 죄송합니다.). When to use it: 직원이 자기 쪽 문제를 사과할 때 써요. Note: 대답: That’s all right. (괜찮아요).
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.

Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: There’s a problem with my ___. / It doesn’t work. / I’m sorry about that. / That’s all right. Table (물건 → 문제):

The heater *doesn’t work*. 난방기가 안 돼요.

안 될 때 쓰는 세 가지 말

It *doesn’t work*. 작동이 안 돼요.
It *isn’t working*. (지금) 안 되고 있어요.
It’s *broken*. 고장 났어요.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- doesn’t + 동사원형: 주어가 it·he·she면 doesn’t, I·you·we·they면 don’t. / The heater doesn’t work. 난방기가 안 돼요. / doesn’t 뒤에는 -s 없이: work (works ×)
- 안 될 때 쓰는 세 가지 말: It doesn’t work. 작동이 안 돼요. / It isn’t working. (지금) 안 되고 있어요. / It’s broken. 고장 났어요.
Common mistakes on screen:
- It doesn’t works. → It doesn’t work. (doesn’t 뒤에는 -s 없이 동사원형.)
- The heater don’t work. → The heater doesn’t work. (heater(it) 뒤에는 doesn’t.)
- There’s not hot water. → There’s no hot water. (명사 앞에서 ‘없다’는 no.)
- The lock is break. → The lock is broken. (고장 난 상태는 broken.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.
points: doesn’t + 동사원형: 주어가 it·he·she면 doesn’t, I·you·we·they면 don’t.The heater doesn’t work. 난방기가 안 돼요.doesn’t 뒤에는 -s 없이: work (works ×)

mistakes: It doesn’t works. → It doesn’t work.
The heater don’t work. → The heater doesn’t work.
There’s not hot water. → There’s no hot water.
The lock is break. → The lock is broken.

steps.note: 예) heater / doesn’t work → There’s a problem with my heater. It doesn’t work. · 선생님이 직원 역할로 대답해요.
steps.teach:
Situation drill. Note on screen: 예) heater / doesn’t work → There’s a problem with my heater. It doesn’t work. · 선생님이 직원 역할로 대답해요. Items (situation → model answer): heater → doesn’t work | door lock → is broken | air conditioner → isn’t working | light → doesn’t turn on.
Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): wrapping up today.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). Then call finish_session.

This is the start of session 2 of "It doesn’t work." (문제가 있어요); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "There’s a problem with my ___." / "It doesn’t work." / "I’m sorry about that.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 문제 말하기: "The air conditioner isn’t working." (에어컨이 작동이 안 돼요., 보통); "There’s no hot water." (온수가 안 나와요., 보통); "The room is too noisy." (방이 너무 시끄러워요., 보통)
- 부탁하고 답 듣기: "Could you send someone?" (사람 좀 보내 주시겠어요?, 정중); "Can I change rooms?" (방을 바꿀 수 있을까요?, 보통); "We’ll fix it right away." (바로 고쳐 드릴게요., 정중); "Thank you for your patience." (기다려 주셔서 감사합니다., 정중)
- 사과에 답하기: "That’s all right." (괜찮아요., 보통); "It happens." (그럴 수도 있죠., 친근)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

boxes: 방에서 생기는 문제

The window doesn’t *shut*. 창문이 안 닫혀요.
The door doesn’t *lock*. 문이 안 잠겨요.
a *loud* *pipe* 시끄러운 배관 · a *spare* blanket 여분 담요
sorry about · sorry to hear

I’m sorry *about* that. (우리 쪽 문제라) 죄송해요. — 직원이 사과할 때
I’m sorry *to hear* that. 안됐네요. — 남의 안 좋은 소식에(3과)
사과에 답하기: That’s all right. · It happens.
steps.blank:

steps.teach:
Tips on screen:
- 방에서 생기는 문제: The window doesn’t shut. 창문이 안 닫혀요. / The door doesn’t lock. 문이 안 잠겨요. / a loud pipe 시끄러운 배관 · a spare blanket 여분 담요
- sorry about · sorry to hear: I’m sorry about that. (우리 쪽 문제라) 죄송해요. — 직원이 사과할 때 / I’m sorry to hear that. 안됐네요. — 남의 안 좋은 소식에(3과) / 사과에 답하기: That’s all right. · It happens.
Fill-in-the-blank dialogue on screen: A: There’s a ___ with my heater. It ___ work. B: I’m ___ about that. We’ll fix it right ___. / A: Okay, thank you. B: Thank you for your ___. / 낱말 상자: problem · doesn’t · sorry · away · patience
Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): picture words.

Picture words on screen. New: heater (난방기, 히터), air conditioner (에어컨), broken (고장 난, 깨진), noisy (시끄러운), lock (자물쇠; 잠그다), shut (닫다, 닫히다), tap (수도꼭지), pipe (배관, 관), spare (여분의), hot water (뜨거운 물, 온수). Review words: light (전등, 불), fix (고치다).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

items: There’s a problem with my room.
There’s no hot water in the shower.
Could I have a spare blanket?
The new room is very quiet.
steps.teach:
Word list on screen: problem (문제) — "There’s a problem with my room."; work ((기계가) 작동하다(앞에서는 ‘(날·시간이) 괜찮다; 일하다’)) — "The heater doesn’t work."; send (보내다) — "Could you send someone?"; someone (누군가) — "Someone is at the door."; patience (참을성, 기다려 줌) — "Thank you for your patience."; loud ((소리가) 큰) — "The music is too loud."; right away (바로, 곧장(right은 앞에서는 ‘맞는, 옳은’)) — "We’ll fix it right away."; shower (샤워(기)) — "There’s no hot water in the shower."; blanket (담요) — "Could I have a spare blanket?"; quiet (조용한) — "The new room is very quiet.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): questions about the learner's own life.

items: You’re at a hotel. The heater doesn’t work. What do you say?
There’s a problem with my heater. It doesn’t work.
I work at the front desk. “I’m sorry about that.” What do you say?
Your hotel room is too noisy. What can you ask?
Can I change rooms? / Could you send someone?
At home, what do you do when something doesn’t work?
I fix it myself. / I call someone.
Have you ever had a problem at a hotel?
Yes, once. The ___ didn’t work. / No, never.
steps.teach:
My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "You’re at a hotel. The heater doesn’t work. What do you say?" (hint on screen: There’s a problem with my heater. It doesn’t work.)
- "I work at the front desk. “I’m sorry about that.” What do you say?" (hint on screen: That’s all right. / Thank you.)
- "Your hotel room is too noisy. What can you ask?" (hint on screen: Can I change rooms? / Could you send someone?)
- "At home, what do you do when something doesn’t work?" (hint on screen: I fix it myself. / I call someone.)
- "Have you ever had a problem at a hotel?" (hint on screen: Yes, once. The ___ didn’t work. / No, never.)
Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short reading.

steps.title: A Quiet Room
steps.text: After breakfast, Jiwoo moved to Room 508 *along with* her heavy suitcase. The new room was warm and quiet. The heater worked well, and there was plenty of hot water. The big window reflected the morning sun. *Other than* a little noise from the elevator, everything was perfect. The front desk also sent up a spare blanket and some cookies with a note, “Thank you for your patience.” Jiwoo smiled. “My first problem abroad, and I fixed it in English!” Chloe laughed. “It happens to everyone. Now let’s go see my city!”
steps.gloss: along with ~와 함께 · reflect 비추다, 반사하다 · other than ~ 말고는 · send up (위층으로) 올려 보내다 · note 쪽지 · plenty of 넉넉한
questions: What did the front desk send up?
What was the only small problem in the new room?
steps.teach:
Reading on screen: "A Quiet Room". Text: "After breakfast, Jiwoo moved to Room 508 along with her heavy suitcase. The new room was warm and quiet. The heater worked well, and there was plenty of hot water. The big window reflected the morning sun. Other than a little noise from the elevator, everything was perfect. The front desk also sent up a spare blanket and some cookies with a note, “Thank you for your patience.” Jiwoo smiled. “My first problem abroad, and I fixed it in English!” Chloe laughed. “It happens to everyone. Now let’s go see my city!”" Words: along with ~와 함께 · reflect 비추다, 반사하다 · other than ~ 말고는 · send up (위층으로) 올려 보내다 · note 쪽지 · plenty of 넉넉한.
Read the text aloud exactly as written at a natural pace, then ask the questions one at a time: "What did the front desk send up?" / "What was the only small problem in the new room?". React to their answers; if one is not right, point to the sentence. You may add one short personal question linked to the reading. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the 'I can' check-out.

items: ‘There’s a problem with my ___.’로 무엇에 문제가 있는지 말할 수 있어요.
‘It doesn’t work.’로 안 되는 것을 설명하고 부탁할 수 있어요.

steps.teach:
Check-out. The 'I can' list on screen:
- ‘There’s a problem with my ___.’로 무엇에 문제가 있는지 말할 수 있어요.
- ‘It doesn’t work.’로 안 되는 것을 설명하고 부탁할 수 있어요.

Ask the learner to pick one and show it by saying a sentence; react and praise specifically. Then end like a person: ask how this lesson felt, react, say that the next lesson comes next, and say a warm goodbye. Then call finish_session.

steps.title: 여행 이야기
steps.title_en: Where did you go on your last trip?
steps.goal: 다녀온 여행을 말하고 어땠는지, 가장 좋았던 것 말하기
steps.scene_desc: 4월 말 저녁, 토론토의 작은 호텔 방. 창가 의자에 앉은 지우가 노트북 화면 속 마야와 영상 통화를 하며 손바닥 위 작은 조개껍데기를 들어 보여 줌(화면·창밖에 글자 없이)
steps.teach:
This is the very start of the class. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up, like a real tutor meeting a student: greet the learner by name (if this is your first class together, introduce yourself as your class notes say). Then have a short, genuine small-talk chat of about two to four exchanges: how they are, their day, the weather, or something you know about them. React to what they actually say with real interest, and share a small, ordinary thing about yourself now and then. Keep it easy for their level; Korean answers are fine here, just respond to them naturally.
2) Then bridge from the chat to today's topic: "Where did you go on your last trip?" (여행 이야기). Goal: 다녀온 여행을 말하고 어땠는지, 가장 좋았던 것 말하기. Today's scene: 4월 말 저녁, 토론토의 작은 호텔 방. 창가 의자에 앉은 지우가 노트북 화면 속 마야와 영상 통화를 하며 손바닥 위 작은 조개껍데기를 들어 보여 줌(화면·창밖에 글자 없이). Link it to something from the chat if you can, and say in a sentence what we'll do: learn 3 expressions, then hear a short scene.
3) Call next_step only after the learner has answered and seems ready.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 1, "Where did you go on your last trip?".

steps.en: Where did you go on your last trip?
steps.when: 상대가 다녀온 여행을 물을 때 써요. 지나간 일이라 did + 동사원형.
steps.extra: 대답: I went to Busan. · I went to a small island.
steps.teach:
Expression 1 of 3: "Where did you go on your last trip?" (지난 여행 때 어디 갔어요?). When to use it: 상대가 다녀온 여행을 물을 때 써요. 지나간 일이라 did + 동사원형. Note: 대답: I went to Busan. · I went to a small island.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 2, "I went to ___.".

steps.when: 다녀온 곳을 말해요. go의 과거형은 *went*.
steps.extra: I went to Toronto. · I went to the lake.
steps.teach:
Expression 2 of 3: "I went to ___." (~에 갔어요.). When to use it: 다녀온 곳을 말해요. go의 과거형은 went. Note: I went to Toronto. · I went to the lake.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): expression 3, "The best part was ___.".

steps.when: 여행에서 가장 좋았던 것을 하나 골라 말해요.
steps.extra: The best part was the food. · The best part was the beach.
steps.teach:
Expression 3 of 3: "The best part was ___." (제일 좋았던 건 ~였어요.). When to use it: 여행에서 가장 좋았던 것을 하나 골라 말해요. Note: The best part was the food. · The best part was the beach.
Teach it like a person, not a drill: set up a tiny real situation (from the warm-up chat or the learner's life if you can), say it, and let the learner say it. The learner fills the blank with their own real word (for example their own name), never by reading the blank. Show it first with your own example. Then really use it together in a short exchange: you each say something, and you answer as yourself (if the learner asks you a question, answer it honestly in a natural way). Fix at most one thing, gently. When they have used it once in that exchange and you have replied to them, call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): the app plays a short scene ("Day Four · 토론토 나흘째 저녁, 마야와 영상 통화") in the characters' own voices — tell them to just listen.

steps.teach:
Useful sentences on screen. Key pattern: Where did you go on your last trip? / How long were you there? / I went to ___. The best part was ___. Table (어디에 갔나 → 무엇을 했나):
- I went to Busan. → I swam at the beach.
- I went to a small island. → I rode a bike.
- I went to Toronto. → I walked by the lake.
- I went to a desert. → I saw wild animals.
Turn two or three rows into quick real-life moments, one at a time (for example: You meet a new neighbor. What do you ask?), let the learner answer, and react to what they say like a person. One task per turn. Do not read labels, arrows or the word pattern aloud. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a short grammar point and common mistakes.

items:
순서대로: *First*, I went to the lake. *Then*, I had dinner.
물을 때는 *did* + 동사원형: Where *did* you *go*?

go → *went* · take → *took* · see → *saw* · buy → *bought*
be동사: It *was* amazing. · How long *were* you there?
errors: Where you went on your last trip?
Where did you go on your last trip?
물을 때는 did를 넣고 동사원형 go.
steps.teach:
Grammar on screen:
- 과거형으로 이어 말하기: 순서대로: First, I went to the lake. Then, I had dinner. / 물을 때는 did + 동사원형: Where did you go?
- 자주 쓰는 불규칙 과거형: go → went · take → took · see → saw · buy → bought / be동사: It was amazing. · How long were you there?
Common mistakes on screen:
- Where you went on your last trip? → Where did you go on your last trip? (물을 때는 did를 넣고 동사원형 go.)
- Where did you went? → Where did you go? (did 뒤에는 동사원형.)
- I went to there. → I went there. (there 앞에는 to를 쓰지 않아요.)
- I went by me. → I went by myself. (‘혼자’는 by myself.)
Explain each point in one or two plain sentences with a short example, ideally about the learner. Then pick two of the mistakes: say the wrong sentence, let the learner fix it, and confirm. Keep it light, then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a quick situation drill.

Give them one at a time as a tiny situation in simple English and let the learner answer. Recast once if needed. Keep it lively, with a quick natural reaction to each answer. After all items, call next_step.

Wrap up session 1 like a person ending a class. Ask in one short question how today's class felt, and react to their answer. Then praise one specific thing they did today, say that next time we will learn more expressions on this topic and talk about their own story, and say a warm goodbye (use today's expression if it fits). steps.teach:
This is the start of session 2 of "Where did you go on your last trip?" (여행 이야기); it may be a different day from session 1. Do not start the textbook yet.
1) Warm-up: greet the learner by name and have a short, genuine small-talk chat of two or three exchanges (how they have been, or follow up on something they told you before). React to what they say.
2) Then bridge to a quick review of last time's expressions: "Where did you go on your last trip?" / "I went to ___." / "The best part was ___.". For each, give a tiny real situation and let them answer; react naturally. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): more expressions on the same topic.

steps.teach:
More expressions on this topic (on screen):
- 여행 더 묻기: "How long were you there?" (거기 얼마나 있었어요?, 보통); "Who did you go with?" (누구랑 갔어요?, 보통)
- 대답하기: "For a week." (일주일요., 보통); "I went by myself." (혼자 갔어요., 보통); "I took a lot of pictures." (사진을 많이 찍었어요., 보통)
- 어땠는지 말하기: "The food was amazing." (음식이 정말 맛있었어요., 친근); "The weather wasn’t great." (날씨는 별로였어요., 보통); "I’d love to go back." (꼭 다시 가고 싶어요., 보통); "I’d recommend it." (추천해요., 보통)
Do not read the whole list. Pick three or four that fit the learner's life, say each and let them say it, and use one or two in a quick real exchange with them. Mention casual (친근) vs polite (정중) where it helps. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): tips and a fill-in-the-blank dialogue.

Mention each tip in one or two sentences, linked to the learner if you can. Then do the fill-in-the-blank dialogue: read it line by line, pausing at each blank so they can fill it, and confirm. Then call next_step.

Picture words on screen. New: travel (여행하다), vacation (휴가), holiday (휴일, 휴가), tour (관광, 투어), sightseeing (구경, 관광), museum (박물관, 미술관), souvenir (기념품), animal (동물), desert (사막), bar (막대 모양의 것(초콜릿 바 등)), beach (해변), picture (사진, 그림).
Go through about six, new ones first: call highlight_word with the word, say it, and let the learner say it. Now and then ask a tiny real question with the word (for example: Are you a morning person?) and react to the answer. Then call next_step.
What comes next (after you call next_step): a word list.

Word list on screen: trip (여행) — "How was your trip?"; abroad (해외로, 해외에서) — "my first trip abroad"; local (그 지역의, 동네의) — "I love the local food."; foreign (외국의) — "a foreign city"; culture (문화) — "I’m into Korean culture."; myself (나 자신) — "I went by myself."; return (돌아오다) — "I returned home on Sunday."; wild (야생의) — "wild animals"; pleasant (기분 좋은, 쾌적한) — "a pleasant walk"; shore (물가, 호숫가·바닷가) — "We walked along the shore.".
Pick three or four, say their example phrases, then ask the learner to make one short sentence about their own life with one of them, and respond to what they say. Then call next_step.

My story: this is the most conversational part of the lesson. Questions on screen:
- "Where did you go on your last trip?" (hint on screen: I went to ___.)
- "How long were you there?" (hint on screen: For ___ days. / For a week.)
- "What was the best part?" (hint on screen: The best part was ___.)

Ask them one at a time as a real conversation: react to each answer with genuine interest, add a short follow-up question or a bit about yourself when it feels natural, then move on. Ask for a full sentence and recast once if needed. If they don't want to answer, accept that or an imagined answer without asking again. Then call next_step.

steps.title: A Rainy Day Four
steps.text: It rained throughout the morning, so Chloe and Jiwoo went to a big museum. There was a room about old kings and queens. Jiwoo saw a royal crown and a small model of a castle. In the afternoon, the rain stopped *at last*. They *set out* for a beach by the lake. The sand was cold, but Jiwoo found a pretty shell. “My favorite souvenir!” she said. Then a wild animal ran across the path. It was a raccoon! Soon the wind got strong, so they *turned around* and went back to town. That night, Daniel sent a message: “I’m home in Chicago next week. Come and visit!” Maybe Jiwoo will.
